people.name: Mouha ou Hammou Zayani
people.aliasesRaw: Tamazight: Muḥa u Ḥemmu Aẓayyi · Moha ou Hammou · Mouha ou Hammou Zaïani / Zaïani / Zayani · Moha ou Hammou Azayi · Fr. archives: 'Moha ou Hammou', 'le caïd Hammou', 'Hammou des Zaïanes', 'le chef zaïan' · Sp.: Mohamed Hammou, 'el caíd Hammu', 'los zayanes' · Ar.: محا أو حمو الزياني
aliases: Mouha ou Hammou Zaïani / Zaïani / Zayani
people.born: c. 1857 or c. 1863, Middle Atlas — not established
people.died: 27 March 1921 (some accounts spring 1921 without exact date), Azlag n'Tazemmourt / Azelag N'Tazemourte, Middle Atlas
people.oneLine: Qaid of the Zaian confederation, appointed by the Makhzen in the 1870s–80s; led the Zaian war against France 1914–1921 and commanded at El Herri.
people.contestedPoints: Year of his qaid appointment (1877 / 1880 / 1886). Birth year. Whether his son Hassan personally killed him or whether he died in a fight against a faction his sons had joined. Zaian casualty figures at El Herri (the French count of 182 is a French battlefield count). Whether the makhzen investiture made him an agent of the sultan or ratified power he already held.
people.body:
> **Evidence note.** The best evidence on this man is, unavoidably, **French military evidence** — he is documented most densely by the institution trying to destroy him. That asymmetry shapes everything below and is flagged where it bites. Amazigh oral tradition (*izlan*, *timdyazin*) is a real and largely untapped counter-archive; none of it has been consulted directly for this dossier.

## Identity

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Clan | Imazhan, within the Ayt Harkat section |
| Confederation | **Zaian** (Izayyan), Central Middle Atlas, seat at **Khénifra** |
| Office | Qaid of the Ayt Yaʿqoub half of the Zaian confederation, by Makhzen investiture under Hassan I |
| Language | Central Atlas Tamazight |
| Confederation size | French estimates of 4,000–4,200 tents under his authority. **A French estimate, not a census.** |

## The appointment — and why it is misread

By the account that circulates in the reference literature, Mouha travelled to the Tadla with his cousin Bouhassous and was presented to **Hassan I** through the marabout **Sidi Ben Dawd Sherqawi** of the Sherqawa zawiya of Boujad. Hassan invested him as qaid, with a black cloak, a detachment of sharifian infantry (a figure of 300 appears), and artillery.

**Date disputed:** 1877, 1880 and 1886 all appear in reference works of comparable authority. Unresolved.

**Interpretive point, stated as interpretation.** French Protectorate ethnography classified the Middle Atlas as *bled es-siba* — dissidence — and Mouha as an *insoumis* chief. But he held a Makhzen commission, obtained through a recognised religious intermediary, from the sultan. He was not outside the Moroccan political order; he was **inside it, in the position that order actually offered to a mountain confederation** — autonomous power ratified by sharifian investiture. What changed in 1912 was not his status but the state claiming his allegiance.

> **Terminology.** *Insoumis*, *dissident*, *rebelle* in Résidence Générale and Bureau des Affaires Indigènes usage denote an armed leader outside **French** authority. They carry no implication of illegitimacy in Moroccan terms, and reproducing them as description rather than as evidence of French filing categories is a category error.

## Relationship with the sultans

| Sultan | Relationship | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Hassan I | Invested him as qaid; Mouha sought the investiture | Established, date disputed |
| Abdelaziz | Continued autonomy; no recorded rupture | Thin |
| Abdelhafid | His daughter **Rabha** reportedly married Abdelhafid | Single-source assertion; needs corroboration |
| Moulay Youssef | Sultan in whose name France fought him after 1912 — the central irony of the Zaian war | Established |

After 1912 France waged war on him **in the sultan's name**, under the Treaty of Fez. He did not renounce the sultanate; he refused the French administration exercising it. This distinction is what French reporting collapses and what Moroccan historiography emphasises.

## The Zaian War, 1914–1921

| Date | Event | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 12 June 1914 | French occupy **Khénifra** (Henrys) | Mouha withdraws rather than defend the town |
| 13 Nov 1914 | **El Herri** — Laverdure's column destroyed | See event dossier |
| Nov 1914 | Khénifra invested; French garrison reinforced to c. 7,000 by month's end | French figure |
| May 1915 | **Sidi Sliman** — French counter-offensive under Garnier-Duplessix; c. 300 Zaian dead | French figure |
| June 1917 | Junction at **Assaka Nidji**; trans-Atlas route opened | Strategic turning point |
| 9 Aug 1918 | **Gaouz** — French losses given as 238 killed, 68 wounded | French figure |
| June 1920 | His sons **Hassan** and **Amharoq** submit to **Poeymirau**; c. 3,000 tents follow | Reportedly on his own advice |
| 27 March 1921 | Killed at Azlag n'Tazemmourt | See Death |
| Sept 1921 | Three-pronged French attack near **El Bekrit** ends organised Zaian resistance | |

**On the 1920 submissions.** The reference literature states his sons submitted *on his advice*. If true it reframes him — not a leader fought to annihilation but one who calculated that the confederation's survival required submission while he personally would not make it. **Evidence strength: single-source assertion.** It should be tested against the Bureau des Affaires Indigènes reports for Khénifra, 1920.

## Military method

- **Mobility over position.** He gave up Khénifra in 1914 without a defensive battle. Towns were French assets; the confederation's asset was the mountain.
- **Concentration only on favourable ground.** El Herri is the exception that proves it: he engaged in strength only once a small, exposed, retreating column presented itself.
- **Confederal recruitment.** At El Herri the force included Mrabtin, Ayt Harkat, Ayt Ischak and Ayt Ichkern elements — not a standing army but a coalition assembled on a specific occasion, which is why French estimates of his strength swing so wildly.
- **Constraint.** Cut off from machine guns and artillery. The French export-control effort against arms into the Middle Atlas was, by French assessment, largely effective. Captured French weapons were therefore politically as well as militarily valuable: after El Herri he **displayed captured arms to neighbouring tribes**, and recruitment rose.

## German and Ottoman contact

During the First World War Germany, operating largely through its embassy in **Madrid**, attempted to raise Morocco against France: money smuggled in (a figure of up to 600,000 pesetas per month appears in the literature), arms, advisers, Foreign Legion deserters, and propaganda in Arabic, French and Middle Atlas Tamazight. The Ottoman Empire supplied training and religious framing.

**Assessment:** by both French and later academic reading, largely ineffective — far short of the general jihad the planners wanted. But the effort is why the Zaian war is legible in **German and Spanish** archives as well as French, and it is the reason Spanish-zone material is relevant to a Middle Atlas war fought entirely in the French zone.

Key academic thread: **Edmund Burke III, "Moroccan Resistance, Pan-Islam and German War Strategy, 1914–1918", *Francia* 3 (1975), 434–464.**

## Death — investigated, not repeated

The standard statement is that he was killed on **27 March 1921** at Azlag n'Tazemmourt in a fight against forces led by his own son **Hassan**, who had submitted to the French the previous year.

The versions do not agree:

| Version | Content | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Common encyclopedic | Killed in combat with his son Hassan's forces | Widely repeated |
| French operational | Killed in a clash with a "partisan" (French-allied Berber) party during operations; France did not kill him directly | Consistent with French practice of fighting through allied contingents |
| Some accounts | "Spring 1921", no precise date | Suggests the exact date is a later fixing |
| Moroccan commemorative | Martyr's death in resistance; the fratricidal element is present but de-emphasised | |

**What is established:** he died in early 1921, in the Middle Atlas, in an armed clash, and not in a set-piece battle against French regulars. He is buried at Ben Cherro near Tamalakt, where a tomb, mosque and mausoleum stand.

**What is not established:** whether his son struck the blow, or commanded the party, or was merely present in the opposing alignment. These are three different claims and the sources do not distinguish them. **Do not treat the fratricide as a documented fact.**

**Why it matters:** the fratricide version is narratively useful to *both* sides — to the French as proof that resistance collapsed from within, to a certain Moroccan reading as tragedy that absolves the collaborating half of the family of intent. That both sides benefit from a story is a reason to check it.

**Verification target:** French operational reports and the Khénifra Bureau des Affaires Indigènes political bulletins, March–April 1921. SHD sous-série **GR 3H**. `ARCHIVAL REFERENCE NOT YET VERIFIED`.

## Assessments by nationality

**French.** Respectful and hostile at once. He is the *chef* whose destruction justified a decade of operations, and after El Herri he became the measure of Berber military capacity. Lyautey's correspondence after El Herri shows genuine strategic alarm. The residency's framing — a feudal chief holding tribes by force, whose fall would free them — is contradicted by its own reporting of how long resistance lasted after his death.

**Spanish.** Peripheral. He appears in Spanish material via the German-Madrid channel and as a comparative reference in Rif war discussion.

**Moroccan.** A national resistance figure; El Herri is a founding episode of the resistance canon. The 1991 obelisk at El Herri lists 182 Moroccan dead — and **contains errors**, giving 700 French dead (against the French count of 623) and dating the battle to 1912. A commemorative monument is not a source.

**Amazigh.** Increasingly claimed as a specifically Amazigh figure whose resistance was written out of an Arab-nationalist independence narrative. This is a live and legitimate historiographical argument, and it is also a present-day political argument. Both should be stated.

## Historical assessment

**Established:** Zaian qaid by Makhzen investiture under Hassan I; led Zaian resistance from 1914; commanded at El Herri 13 Nov 1914; his sons submitted June 1920; he died in the Middle Atlas in early 1921; organised Zaian resistance ended Sept 1921.

**Highly probable:** his authority was confederal and negotiated, not autocratic; French estimates of his strength are unreliable in both directions.

**Disputed:** appointment date; birth year; the fratricide; the claim that he advised his sons to submit.

**Unknown:** almost everything about his internal politics — how decisions were taken in the Zaian *jemāʿa*, how he financed the war, what he thought he was fighting for in his own words. **No Zaian-side written source has been used in this dossier.** Whether one exists is itself an open question worth pursuing in the Arabic manuscript collections at Rabat.

people.name: Abdelkhalek Torres
people.aliasesRaw: عبد الخالق الطريس · Abdelkhalek Torres · Abd al-Khaliq al-Torres · Sp.: 'Abdeljalak Torres'
people.oneLine: Leader of nationalism in the Spanish zone; founder of the Partido de Reformas Nacionales at Tetouan.
people.contestedPoints: The extent of Spanish (and later Francoist) tolerance or sponsorship of northern nationalism as a lever against France, and how far that compromised the movement.

people.name: Moulay Hassan I
people.aliasesRaw: الحسن بن محمد (al-Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad) · Mawlay al-Hasan al-Awwal · Moulay Hassan I · Mulay Hasan · Muley Hassan (Sp.) · Mouley el-Hassan (Fr. consular usage) · Abū ʿAlī al-Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad · 'the last great sultan' (historiographical epithet, not contemporary)
people.born: 1836 (conventional). Some reference works give 1857 — see Contradictions. Fez.
people.died: 9 June 1894, camp on the Oued el-Abid, Tadla region, returning from the Tafilalt harka. Buried Rabat.
people.oneLine: Alaouite sultan 1873–1894; attempted military and fiscal centralisation of the Makhzen under mounting European financial and territorial pressure.
people.contestedPoints: Birth year (1836 vs 1857). Exact year Mouha ou Hammou Zayani was made qaid (1877 / 1880 / 1886). Whether the 1893 Glaoui rescue and Krupp cannon story is documented or a literary elaboration by Gavin Maxwell. Whether his reforms failed on their own terms or were destroyed by the debt and protection regimes.

people.name: Emir Abd el-Malek
people.aliasesRaw: عبد الملك · Amir Abd el-Malek · Abd al-Malik al-Jaza'iri · Mulai Abdelmalek · Fr. archives: 'Abd el Malek' · Ottoman documents: Abdulmelik · Sp.: 'Abd-el-Malek'
people.died: not established — his movement is described as sustaining guerrilla war to 1919 and beyond
people.oneLine: Descendant of the Algerian emir Abd el-Kader and a former Ottoman officer; commanded the Ottoman- and German-backed resistance around Taza and the eastern Rif from 1915.
people.contestedPoints: Whether he was a son or a grandson of Abd el-Kader — two named scholars working from the same archives differ. His dates. Whether his movement was independent or 'forced to support the Germans for money and weapons'. His fate after 1918.

people.name: Ba Ahmed ibn Musa
people.aliasesRaw: أحمد بن موسى · Ahmad ibn Musa · Ba Ahmed · Ba Hmad · Fr.: 'le grand vizir Ba Ahmed'
people.oneLine: Chamberlain and grand vizier; concealed Hassan I's death in 1894 and ruled Morocco as regent for Abdelaziz until 1900.
people.contestedPoints: Whether his regency preserved the Makhzen or hollowed it out by excluding the sultan from government. His personal wealth and the Bahia palace.

people.name: Assou Oubasslam
people.aliasesRaw: عسو أوباسلام · Assou Ou Basslam · Assou u Baslam · Aassou Oubasslam · Fr.: 'Assou ou Ba Slam, chef des Aït Atta'
aliases: Assou ou Ba Slam, chef des Aït Atta
people.oneLine: Aït Atta commander at the siege of Bougafer (Jbel Saghro) in 1933, one of the last organised resistances to the French conquest.
people.contestedPoints: The terms on which Bougafer ended — negotiated terms or surrender. Casualties on both sides. Whether French aerial bombardment of civilians occurred, as Moroccan and Amazigh accounts hold.

people.name: Abderrahim Bouabid
people.aliasesRaw: عبد الرحيم بوعبيد · Abderrahim Bouabid
people.oneLine: Istiqlal then UNFP/USFP leader; economics minister at independence and the principal figure of the legal opposition until his death.
people.contestedPoints: The 1981 imprisonment over his position on the Western Sahara referendum — the limits of permitted dissent under Hassan II.

people.name: Hassan II
people.aliasesRaw: الحسن الثاني · Moulay Hassan ben Mohammed · Hassan II
people.oneLine: King 1961–1999; presided over the Years of Lead, two coup attempts, the Green March and the Western Sahara war.
people.contestedPoints: Command responsibility for the 1958–59 Rif repression, the 1965 Casablanca killings, Ben Barka, Tazmamart, and the disappearances. Almost every major question of this reign is contested and much of the record is closed.

people.name: Alphonse Juin
people.aliasesRaw: Alphonse Pierre Juin · Maréchal Juin
people.oneLine: Resident-General 1947–1951; confronted Mohammed V directly and began the campaign to isolate him from the Istiqlal.
people.contestedPoints: The extent to which he built the coalition of pashas and qaids later used to depose the sultan in 1953.

people.name: Mohamed Oufkir
people.aliasesRaw: محمد أوفقير · Mohamed Oufkir · General Oufkir
people.died: 16 August 1972, Rabat — official cause suicide; disputed
people.oneLine: French army officer who became interior minister and defence minister; central to the repression of the 1960s and to the Ben Barka affair; died after the 1972 coup attempt.
people.contestedPoints: The manner of his death (multiple gunshot wounds are reported, which is difficult to reconcile with suicide). His personal role in Ben Barka's death. The extent of his authorship of the 1972 coup attempt.

people.name: Charles Mangin
people.aliasesRaw: Charles Marie Emmanuel Mangin · Fr. press: 'le boucher' · 'the Butcher'
people.oneLine: Commanded the column that destroyed Ahmed al-Hiba at Sidi Bou Othmane, 6 September 1912; advocate of the 'Force Noire'.
people.contestedPoints: Casualty figures at Sidi Bou Othmane. His broader doctrine of using African colonial troops, and how it shaped who did the dying in Morocco.

people.name: Harry Maclean
people.aliasesRaw: Harry Aubrey de Vere Maclean · Caid Maclean · Kaid Sir Harry Maclean · Ar.: القائد ماكلين
people.oneLine: Scottish officer who commanded and trained the Moroccan sultan's army from the 1870s to 1907; kidnapped by Raisuni.
people.contestedPoints: Whether he served the sultan or British policy, and how far the two diverged. His influence over Abdelaziz. The terms of his ransom in 1907-08.

people.name: Samuel Gummere
people.aliasesRaw: Samuel Rene Gummere · Consul-General then Minister to Morocco
people.oneLine: American diplomat at Tangier during the Perdicaris affair of 1904 and the first US Minister to Morocco.
people.contestedPoints: How far the 'Perdicaris alive or Raisuli dead' telegram reflected policy as against domestic electioneering by Roosevelt.

people.name: Bou Hamara
people.aliasesRaw: بو حمارة ('the man on the she-donkey') · Jilali ben Driss al-Zarhuni al-Yusufi · Jilali Ben Driss Zerhouni · El Rogui / al-Rūgī ('the pretender') · Sp.: 'El Roghi', 'el Pretendiente' · Fr.: 'le Rogui Bou Hamara'
aliases: بو حمارة (the man on the she-donkey)
people.died: September 1909 (2 September per one account), Fez
people.oneLine: Former Makhzen clerk who claimed to be the sultan's elder brother and ran a rival state in northeastern Morocco 1902–1909.
people.contestedPoints: Whether he genuinely claimed to be Moulay Mohammed or was so identified by his followers. The terms of the mining concessions he granted to Spanish and French interests. The manner of his execution — the 'fed to lions' story is repeated but poorly sourced.

people.name: Mohammed ben Abdelkrim El Khattabi
people.aliasesRaw: محمد بن عبد الكريم الخطابي · Abd el-Krim · Abd-el-Krim · Abdelkrim · Abd al-Karim al-Khattabi · Sp. archives: 'Abd-el-Krim', 'el cabecilla', 'el jefe rebelde' · Fr.: 'l'émir du Rif' · Tarifit: Muḥemmed n ʿEbdkrim Lxṭṭabi
people.oneLine: Qadi and Spanish-administration official who led the Rif war 1921–1926 and headed the Rif Republic; the most heavily documented Moroccan resistance figure in European archives.
people.contestedPoints: Whether the Rif Republic was a state, a proto-state or a confederation using modern vocabulary. Silvestre's death (suicide vs killed vs unknown). Annual casualty figures (7,875 to 13,363 depending on source and definition). Whether the 1925 attack on the French zone was overreach or a forced choice. His dealings with foreign mining interests.

people.name: Taher Bey
people.aliasesRaw: Tahir Bey · Taher Bey · Yanyalı Tahir Bey · the name appears as both Tahir and Taher in the two principal studies
aliases: the name appears as both Tahir and Taher in the two principal studies
people.oneLine: Ottoman major who headed the Teşkilât-ı Mahsusa mission to Morocco from Madrid, 1914–1916.
people.contestedPoints: Why he was dismissed in early 1916 — the sources say German pressure. Whether his assessments of tribal leaders were accurate or self-serving.

people.name: M'Hammad ben Abdelkrim El Khattabi
people.aliasesRaw: محمد بن عبد الكريم · M'Hamed / Mhamed / M'Hammad Abd el-Krim · Sp.: 'el hermano de Abd-el-Krim'
people.oneLine: Brother of Abd el-Krim; mining engineer trained in Spain, field commander and the Rif Republic's technical and diplomatic organiser.
people.contestedPoints: Division of authority between the brothers. His role in the Republic's foreign contacts and in the mining question.

people.name: Moulay Youssef
people.aliasesRaw: يوسف بن الحسن · Yusef of Morocco · Moulay Youssef ben Hassan
people.oneLine: Sultan 1912–1927; installed by Lyautey after Abdelhafid's abdication and reigned throughout the pacification wars.
people.contestedPoints: Whether he exercised any independent authority. His role, if any, in the Rif war and in the wartime German approaches.

people.name: Ahmed Balafrej
people.aliasesRaw: أحمد بلفريج · Ahmed Balafrej · Fr.: 'Balafrej'
people.oneLine: Istiqlal secretary-general and drafter of the 1944 Independence Manifesto; first foreign minister of independent Morocco.
people.contestedPoints: His authorship share of the 1944 Manifesto. His role in the internationalisation strategy at the UN and in the Arab League.

people.name: Hugo Stoltzenberg
people.aliasesRaw: Hugo Stoltzenberg · Chemische Fabrik Stoltzenberg, Hamburg
people.oneLine: German chemist who supplied Spain with chemical weapons capability for the Rif war, in breach of the Versailles Treaty.
people.contestedPoints: Quantities supplied and delivery dates. The German government's knowledge and involvement. His role in building La Marañosa.

people.name: Dámaso Berenguer
people.aliasesRaw: Dámaso Berenguer y Fusté, conde de Xauen · 'el Alto Comisario'
aliases: Dámaso Berenguer y Fusté, conde de Xauen
people.oneLine: High Commissioner in Morocco 1919–1922; found negligent by the Expediente Picasso and the author of the documented authorisation of chemical munitions.
people.contestedPoints: His degree of responsibility for Silvestre's advance. Whether the amnesty was political protection. The chain of command for chemical weapons after August 1921.

people.name: Philippe Pétain
people.aliasesRaw: Henri Philippe Bénoni Omer Joseph Pétain · Maréchal Pétain
aliases: Henri Philippe Bénoni Omer Joseph Pétain
people.oneLine: Sent to Morocco in 1925 with authority over Lyautey to defeat Abd el-Krim; later head of the Vichy state.
people.contestedPoints: The extent of French participation in, or knowledge of, chemical weapons use in the Rif. Whether his appointment was intended to displace Lyautey.

people.name: Abdelhadi Boutaleb
people.aliasesRaw: عبد الهادي بوطالب · Abdelhadi Boutaleb
people.oneLine: Tutor to Hassan II, minister, ambassador and secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference; a memoirist of the palace.
people.contestedPoints: The reliability of his memoirs, which are among the few insider accounts of the palace and are written by a loyal servant of it.

people.name: Paul Prosper Henrys
people.aliasesRaw: Paul Prosper Henrys · Général Henrys
people.oneLine: Commanded French forces in the Middle Atlas from 1914; took Taza and Khénifra and directed the Zaian war after El Herri.
people.contestedPoints: His prior knowledge of Laverdure's intentions before 13 November 1914. The human cost of the 'submit or starve' policy he adopted afterwards.

people.name: Mohamed Hassan Ouazzani
people.aliasesRaw: محمد بن الحسن الوزاني · Ouazzani · Wazzani · Fr.: 'El Ouezzani'
people.oneLine: Nationalist leader and journalist; split from Allal El Fassi in 1937 to found a rival party, and remained outside Istiqlal thereafter.
people.contestedPoints: The causes of the 1937 split — personal, ideological, or over the movement's relationship to the throne.

people.name: Abdallah Ibrahim
people.aliasesRaw: عبد الله إبراهيم · Abdallah Ibrahim · Abdellah Ibrahim
people.oneLine: Prime minister 1958–1960; led the only government of independent Morocco to attempt a socialist economic programme.
people.contestedPoints: Why his government was dismissed in May 1960 and how far its economic programme had actually gone.

people.name: Joseph-François Poeymirau
people.aliasesRaw: Joseph-François Poeymirau · Général Poeymirau · Fr.: 'Poeymirau le fougueux'
people.oneLine: Succeeded Henrys in the Middle Atlas; established French control of the Moulouya and received the submission of Mouha ou Hammou's sons in 1920.
people.contestedPoints: The terms offered to the Zaian sons in June 1920 — what was promised, and whether it was kept.

people.name: M'barek Bekkay
people.aliasesRaw: المبارك البكاي · M'Barek Bekkai Lahbil · Si Bekkay · Fr.: 'le colonel Bekkay'
people.oneLine: French army officer who resigned as pasha of Sefrou over the 1953 deposition and became independent Morocco's first prime minister.
people.contestedPoints: Whether his appointment in 1955 was a nationalist choice or a compromise designed to reassure France.

people.name: Henri Gouraud
people.aliasesRaw: Henri Joseph Eugène Gouraud · Général Gouraud · 'le manchot' (after losing an arm at Gallipoli)
aliases: le manchot (after losing an arm at Gallipoli)
people.oneLine: Commanded in Mauritania against Ma al-'Aynayn's networks and in Morocco from 1911; later High Commissioner in the Levant.
people.contestedPoints: His conduct of the Mauritanian campaigns and the destruction of Saharan religious centres.

people.name: Mehdi Ben Barka
people.aliasesRaw: المهدي بن بركة · Mehdi Ben Barka · El Mehdi Ben Barka
people.died: Disappeared 29 October 1965, Paris. Body never found; date and manner of death not established.
people.oneLine: Mathematician, Istiqlal then UNFP leader and Tricontinental organiser; abducted in Paris in 1965 and never seen again.
people.contestedPoints: Who ordered it; whether Hassan II authorised it directly; the roles of Oufkir, Dlimi, French police and services, Mossad and the CIA; where the body is. French files remain classified; c. 1,800 CIA documents acknowledged and undisclosed.
people.body:
> **The clearest case in this workspace of an event where the documents exist and are withheld.**

**Established.** Born Rabat 1920; among the youngest signatories of the **Independence Manifesto, 11 January 1944**; tutor to the future Hassan II; left Istiqlal on 25 January 1959 and helped form the **UNFP**; secretary and chair of the preparatory commission for the **Tricontinental Conference** (Havana, January 1966); **abducted in Paris on 29 October 1965** in an operation involving French police officers; never seen again.

**Judicial finding.** A 1967 French trial convicted two officers of kidnapping. The court identified Moroccan Interior Minister **Mohamed Oufkir** as principally responsible. The witness **Georges Figon**, who testified that Oufkir stabbed Ben Barka, was found dead — officially suicide.

**Alleged and unproven.** **Ahmed Dlimi** requesting the operation on the king's behalf. Mossad locating him and supplying logistics (Ronen Bergman, 2018) — `JOURNALISTIC`, based on Israeli sources. Czechoslovak StB contact 1961–1965 (Jan Koura, 2020) — `ACADEMIC`, from StB files, and it complicates the martyrology without touching the responsibility question.

**Unknown.** The location of the body; the manner and exact date of death; whether Hassan II gave a direct order; the full extent of French and American foreknowledge.

**Why he belongs at the centre of Phase IX.** Ben Barka is the point where the independence movement's left wing was physically removed. Everything about the Years of Lead follows from the fact that it could be done in Paris, by a French police operation, and remain officially unresolved sixty years later.

people.name: Augustin Guillaume
people.aliasesRaw: Augustin Léon Guillaume · Général Guillaume
people.oneLine: Resident-General 1951–1954; executed the deposition and exile of Mohammed V in August 1953.
people.contestedPoints: Whether he initiated the deposition, executed a decision taken in Paris, or was carried along by El Glaoui and the notables. All three versions are in circulation.

people.name: Shakib Arslan
people.aliasesRaw: شكيب أرسلان · Shakib Arslan · 'amīr al-bayān' · Fr.: 'l'émir Chekib Arslan'
people.oneLine: Druze-Lebanese pan-Islamic publicist based in Geneva who internationalised the Moroccan campaign against the 1930 Berber dahir.
people.contestedPoints: The extent of his direct influence on the Moroccan nationalist leadership as against parallel development. His wartime political alignments.

people.name: Juan Picasso González
people.aliasesRaw: Juan Picasso González · 'el general Picasso' · the Expediente Picasso
people.oneLine: Spanish general appointed to investigate the Annual disaster; author of the inquiry that remains the primary documentary base for it.
people.contestedPoints: How much of the original file survives and in what condition. What his brief permitted him to investigate and what it excluded.

people.name: Thami El Glaoui
people.aliasesRaw: التهامي الڣلاوي · Thami el Glaoui · T'hami El Glaoui · Si Thami · 'le Glaoui' · 'the Lord of the Atlas' (English literary coinage, Gavin Maxwell) · 'le Pacha de Marrakech' · Sp.: 'el Glaui'
aliases: the Lord of the Atlas (English literary coinage
people.oneLine: Pasha of Marrakech 1907–1956 and the Protectorate's principal Moroccan intermediary in the south; central actor in the 1953 deposition of Mohammed V.
people.contestedPoints: Whether the 1893 Telouet rescue and Krupp cannon story is documented or literary. The size of his fortune (the $50m figure is an estimate of unclear origin). Whether the 1953 deposition was his initiative or a French operation using him. Whether his 1955 submission was conviction, calculation, or coercion by his own family.

people.name: Ali Amhaouch
people.aliasesRaw: علي أمهاوش · Sidi Ali Amhaouch · Ali Amhawch · Fr.: 'le marabout Amhaouch', 'le chef religieux des Aït Sokhman'
aliases: le chef religieux des Aït Sokhman
people.died: 1918, before the end of the Zaian war; natural causes per the standard account
people.oneLine: Darqawi-linked religious leader of the Middle Atlas whose spiritual authority organised resistance across tribal boundaries.

people.aliasesRaw: Alfonso XIII de Borbón · 'el Rey Alfonso'

people.name: Ma al-'Aynayn
people.aliasesRaw: ماء العينين · Ma al-ʿAynayn · Ma el Ainïn · Ma El Aininn · Cheikh Ma el Ainín (Fr.) · Ma-el-Ainin (Sp.) · birth name Muḥammad Muṣṭafā wuld Muḥammad Faḍil · Fr. archives: 'le marabout Ma el Aïnin', 'le cheikh du Sahara'

people.oneLine: Sufi shaykh, scholar and Makhzen khalifa of the Sahara; founder of Smara and organiser of Saharan resistance to French expansion.

The Spanish role in arming him — asserted in French reporting, an interested claim. His date of birth. The real strength of his following.
people.body:
> **Evidence note.** This dossier is thinner than it should be. The essential scholarship — the Persistence-of-resistance literature in French, and **François Beslay / Attilio Gaudio** and the *Le mouvement hibiste* volume (Presses universitaires de Rennes) — was **not retrievable** in this session (robots restrictions on Persée and OpenEdition). Treat the whole dossier as provisional and the reading list as the priority action.

## Identity

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Lineage | Ahl Ma al-ʿAynayn; son of Muḥammad Faḍil, of the Qadiriyya-Fadiliyya |
| Role | ʿālim, Sufi shaykh, prolific author, arbitrator, city-founder, war leader |
| Foundation | **Smara** (al-Smāra), Saguia el-Hamra, from c. 1898 — a built stone town with a library, in territory of tents |
| Makhzen office | **Khalifa of the Sahara**, appointed by Hassan I, 1887 |
| Sons | **Ahmed al-Hiba** ("the Blue Sultan"), **Merebbi Rebbu**, and others — several of whom warrant dossiers |

## Why he matters, stated plainly

He is the figure through whom the Moroccan state's claim to the Sahara was exercised in the decades when it could not be garrisoned — and therefore the figure on whom a very large modern political question rests. That makes his historiography **unusually contaminated in every direction**:

| Reader | Interest |
|---|---|
| Moroccan | Proof of Makhzen sovereignty over the Sahara through investiture and *bayʿa* |
| Sahrawi nationalist | Proof of an autonomous Saharan polity that owed the sultan religious deference, not political subjection |
| French colonial | Proof that the region was ungoverned and available |
| Spanish | Proof that Spanish coastal claims faced no organised state |

All four readings use the same handful of facts. This dossier states the facts and refuses the conclusion.

## The Makhzen relationship

**Established:** Hassan I appointed him his representative over the Saharan territories by dahir. **The date is disputed — 1879 and 1887 both appear in reference literature of comparable authority.** The 1887 dating links the appointment to Spanish occupation at Dakhla; the 1879 dating places it earlier and independent of it. **This is not a trivial discrepancy:** it changes whether the appointment was a reaction to European encroachment or a prior assertion of Moroccan sovereignty, which is exactly the point at issue in the modern territorial argument. Under Abdelaziz, and more clearly under Abdelhafid, the relationship continued: he received arms and subsidies from Fez and Marrakech and acted as the Makhzen's instrument against French advance from Mauritania and Senegal.

**Disputed:** what "khalifa" delegated. Two defensible readings:

- **Delegated sovereignty** — he governed, taxed and made war *for* the sultan, within a recognised imperial framework; his authority was derivative.
- **Ratified autonomy** — the Makhzen recognised a power it did not create and could not command, in exchange for the recognition of sharifian religious primacy. His authority was his own.

The honest position is that **both are partly true and the balance shifted over time**, moving toward autonomy as the Makhzen weakened after 1900. Any source that resolves this cleanly in either direction should be read for its politics.

## Smara

Founding a stone town with a library and a mosque in the Saguia el-Hamra from the 1890s was a **political act**: it asserted permanence and statehood in a landscape European powers classified as empty. Spanish and French reporting registered it as such.

The French razed Smara in 1913. That act — the deliberate destruction of the physical proof of a Saharan polity — is worth its own event dossier.

## Resistance and the French advance

From the 1900s the French advance from Mauritania (Coppolani, then Gouraud) collided directly with his authority. The assassination of **Xavier Coppolani in 1905** was attributed by French authorities to his circle — an attribution made by the aggrieved party and requiring independent testing.

He supplied, blessed and coordinated Saharan resistance; his sons commanded in the field.

## 1910 — the march north and Tadla

In 1910 he moved north into Morocco proper. Two things are asserted about this and they should be separated:

1. **That he marched to reinforce or replace a failing Makhzen against European encroachment.** Plausible; consistent with his record.
2. **That he claimed the sultanate himself.** Reported, and *disputed*. His son al-Hiba certainly did so in 1912. Whether the father did in 1910 is not established here.

By one account he moved north with an army of around **6,000 men** — a figure of uncertain origin — and his forces were defeated by French troops under **Moinier on 23 June 1910**. He withdrew to **Tiznit**, where he died on **23 October 1910**.

Note the four-month gap between defeat and death, which the compressed versions of this story tend to elide.

## The Spanish arms question

French reporting alleged that Spain supplied him with arms through the southern coast, in breach of Franco-Spanish understanding.

**Status: claim, not fact.** It was made by France, about Spain, at a moment of Franco-Spanish competition over the southern zone. It may be true; Spain had motive and coastline. It requires **Spanish** documentation, and none has been examined here.

Research lead: AHN *Estado*; AGA *Fondo África*; the Spanish Foreign Ministry archive; the Canary Islands commands. `ARCHIVAL REFERENCE NOT YET VERIFIED`.

## The succession: al-Hiba

His son **Ahmed al-Hiba** (b. 9 September 1877, d. 1919), *al-Sulṭān al-Azraq* — the Blue Sultan — proclaimed himself sultan at Tiznit after the Treaty of Fez, entered **Marrakech on 18 August 1912** and was proclaimed there. On **6 September 1912** his army was destroyed at **Sidi Bou Othmane** by Colonel **Charles Mangin** — reported losses around 2,000 tribal fighters against very light French casualties, the standard signature of machine guns and artillery against massed cavalry. He was driven from Taroudant in January 1913, withdrew to Kerdous in the Anti-Atlas, and died there in 1919. His brother **Merebbi Rebbu** succeeded him.

The *hibiste* movement is the direct continuation of Ma al-ʿAynayn's authority and should be researched as one arc, not two.

## Historical assessment

**Established:** Qadiriyya-Fadiliyya lineage; substantial scholarly output; founded Smara; appointed khalifa of the Sahara by Hassan I in 1887; organised Saharan resistance to French expansion; moved north in 1910, was defeated, and died at Tiznit on 23 October 1910; his son al-Hiba took Marrakech in 1912 and lost at Sidi Bou Othmane.

**Highly probable:** his authority rested primarily on religious and scholarly standing, with Makhzen investiture as reinforcement rather than foundation.

**Disputed:** the nature of the khalifa relationship; **the year of his appointment (1879 vs 1887)**; any 1910 claim to the sultanate; Spanish arms supply; his birth year (1830 or 1831; one account gives c. 10 February 1830).

**Unknown:** the scale of his following, his finances, and the content of his own extensive writings — which exist, are catalogued in part, and have **not been used here**. Given that he was a prolific author, using European reports about him in preference to his own texts is a methodological failure this dossier is currently committing and flags as such.

## Priority reading

- *Le mouvement hibiste* (Presses universitaires de Rennes) — ch. I, "Ma el Aïnin, héraut du makhzen ?", whose title alone frames the central question.
- Persée, *Société française d'histoire d'outre-mer*, 1981: "Cheikh Ma el Aïnïn ou la dernière résistance saharienne (1831–1910)".
- The digital library at [cheikh-maelainin.com](http://cheikh-maelainin.com) — manuscripts and works, `PRIMARY_CONTEMPORARY`, produced by the lineage and therefore an interested custodian.

events.body:
> The single most heavily documented episode in this workspace, because it produced a **formal Spanish state inquiry** — the *Expediente Picasso* — and because it was fought under intense international press attention. It is also the episode where the numbers are least agreed.

## Why it matters beyond Morocco

The Rif war destroyed the Spanish constitutional monarchy's credibility, produced Primo de Rivera's dictatorship, and formed the officer corps — **Franco, Sanjurjo, Millán Astray**, the Legion, the Regulares — that made the coup of July 1936. Sebastian Balfour's *Deadly Embrace* is built on that argument. Moroccan history and Spanish history are here **the same history**, and treating them separately produces bad accounts of both.

## Phase 1: the collapse, June–August 1921

**Commanders.** General **Manuel Fernández Silvestre**, Comandante General de Melilla, driving an advance west toward Alhucemas Bay. General **Dámaso Berenguer**, High Commissioner. General **Felipe Navarro**, second at Melilla.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 1 June 1921 | **Monte Abarrán** occupied and lost the same day |
| 17 July | Coordinated Rifian assault on the Spanish position system |
| 21–22 July | **Igueriben** falls after a five-day siege |
| 22 July | Silvestre orders **Annual** evacuated; the withdrawal becomes a rout |
| 22–28 July | Flight toward Melilla under continuous attack; c. 3,000 reach **Monte Arruit** and are besieged |
| 9 August | **Navarro surrenders Monte Arruit** on negotiated terms. The disarmed column is massacred. Roughly **60 of c. 3,000** survive |

**Melilla itself was not taken.** Why not is a genuine question: the city was effectively undefended for days. Explanations range from a deliberate political decision not to provoke total Spanish commitment, to the practical limits of a tribal coalition after a fortnight of continuous fighting and looting.

## The casualty problem

**Rifian casualties: not established.** No systematic count exists on the Rifian side and Spanish estimates of enemy losses in this period are worthless.

## Silvestre's death

| Version | Status |
|---|---|
| Suicide on seeing the position was lost | Most commonly stated; **not documented** |
| Killed during the retreat | Also reported |
| Body never conclusively identified | The underlying problem |

**Status: unknown.** The suicide version serves a narrative purpose — it closes the responsibility question with the responsible officer's self-execution. That does not make it false, but it is a reason for care. Record it as **disputed**.

## The Expediente Picasso

General **Juan Picasso González** was appointed to investigate; his report was delivered in **July 1922**. It is `OFFICIAL` / `PRIMARY_ARCHIVAL` and is the strongest documentary base for the whole disaster.

Findings:

- lines extended far beyond what the available force could hold;
- advance pressed without contingency for counter-attack;
- "friendly" tribes armed by Spain whose loyalty was never secure — and who in the event turned;
- positions dispersed, poorly sited, inadequately supplied with water and ammunition;
- no organised line of retreat, no reserves held back;
- all reserves committed forward to Annual, leaving Melilla stripped.

Picasso judged Silvestre's conduct ***temeraria*** — reckless — and found Berenguer and Navarro negligent.

**What happened to it is the point.** The report reached the Cortes; a responsibilities commission was formed; and **Primo de Rivera's coup of September 1923 shelved both.** Alfonso XIII later amnestied Berenguer, the only officer condemned. An official inquiry established fault and the political system prevented the fault from attaching to anyone.

## The king question

Alfonso XIII was accused of having encouraged Silvestre's advance directly, by telegram, over the heads of the High Commissioner and the government.

**Status: alleged, never proven.** No such telegram has been produced. The allegation was politically explosive in 1921–1923 and contributed materially to the delegitimation of the monarchy, and it remains **unproven**. Record it as an allegation with its political function noted, not as a fact and not as a fabrication.

## Phase 2: the Rif Republic and the war with France, 1921–1926

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 18 Sept 1921 | Rif Republic constituted |
| 1921–24 | Spanish forces confined largely to coastal enclaves; further reverses |
| 1923 | Primo de Rivera's coup; Spanish policy turns to withdrawal to defensible lines, then to a harder war |
| 1923–27 | **Chemical weapons** used — see below |
| Apr 1925 | Rifian offensive into the **French zone** on the Ouergha; Fez threatened |
| 1925 | Lyautey superseded by **Pétain**; Lyautey resigns |
| 8 Sept 1925 | **Alhucemas landing** — large-scale amphibious operation, later studied as a model |
| 1925–26 | Combined Franco-Spanish offensive, 250,000+ troops, aircraft, artillery |
| **26 May 1926** | Abd el-Krim surrenders **to the French** at **Targuist** |

**He surrendered to France, not Spain.** A deliberate choice: the French had not been humiliated at Annual and had no revenge to take, and exile was survivable where Spanish custody might not have been. He was sent to **Réunion**.

## Chemical warfare

A distinct dossier is warranted; the essentials:

| Element | Content | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Agents | Phosgene, diphosgene, chloropicrin, and **mustard gas (yperite)** | Established in scholarship |
| Dates | c. 1921–1927; mustard gas dispersed from aircraft from summer **1924** — a year before the Geneva Protocol took effect | Established |
| Authorisation | Berenguer to War Minister **Marichalar**, **12 August 1921**: he would employ such munitions *"con verdadera fruición"* — "with genuine relish" | Quoted by Balfour from Spanish archives; `Cited by named scholar`, not verified here at document level |
| Supply | Requested from Germany via the chemist **Hugo Stoltzenberg** on 20 August 1921, in breach of Versailles; first delivery 1923. Stoltzenberg later took Spanish nationality and helped build **La Marañosa** (Fábrica Nacional de Productos Químicos) near Madrid | Established in the German and Spanish literature |
| Targets | Civilian population, **zocos** (markets) and rivers — i.e. the food and water system, not military positions | Asserted in scholarship; the specific target lists need archival confirmation |
| Scale figures | c. 127 bombers; c. 1,680 bombs a day; 13 aircraft at Tablada, Seville | **Circulating figures of uncertain provenance. Treat with suspicion until sourced.** |
| Spanish official position | No formal acknowledgement. A 2007 motion in the Congress (Esquerra Republicana) was defeated 33–3 | Established |

**Key literature:** Balfour, *Deadly Embrace* (Oxford, 2002); Kunz & Müller, *Giftgas gegen Abd el Krim* (1990); the memoir of the pilot **Ignacio Hidalgo de Cisneros**, *Cambio de rumbo* — `PRIMARY_CONTEMPORARY`, and written by a man who later became a Republican air force commander, with the political interest that implies.

**Long-term claim, flagged as unresolved:** elevated cancer rates in the Rif have been attributed to the bombardments. This is asserted in Moroccan and Spanish activist literature and in some medical publications. **It is not established here** and would require epidemiological evidence this workspace has not examined.

## The three narratives

Note that Spanish administrative vocabulary files Abd el-Krim as a  — a diminutive by construction, applied to a man who headed a state with an army, a treasury and a foreign policy.

## Unresolved questions

1. Total Spanish dead, on an agreed definition.
2. Silvestre's death.
3. Whether the royal telegrams existed.
4. The full scale and targeting of chemical use — sortie records, munition expenditure, target lists.
5. Rifian casualties, military and civilian. **Effectively unknown, and the gap is not accidental** — nobody with the capacity to count had the interest.
6. Rif Republic internal governance and finance.

## Archival research plan

| Holding | What to request |
|---|---|
| **AGA (Alcalá de Henares)** — *Fondo África*, **Alta Comisaría de España en Marruecos** | 4,990 boxes, 1750–1979. Catalogue-verified in PARES. The core holding |
| **Archivo General Militar de Madrid / Segovia** | Operational files; officer service records; the Melilla command |
| **Expediente Picasso** | The inquiry file itself, and the Cortes responsibilities commission papers |
| **SHD, Vincennes — GR 3H** | Franco-Spanish relations and Spanish zone material, dated 1918–1931 in the SHD guide; French operations 1925–26; military attaché reports from Spain in **série N** |
| **TNA, Kew** | FO 371 — the independent third-party check on both belligerents |
| **German archives** | Stoltzenberg; the Hamburg supply chain |

events.location: El Herri (El Hri, Lehri), c. 15 km south of Khénifra, Middle Atlas
events.summary: A French column of 1,230 men under Lt-Col Laverdure raided Mouha ou Hammou Zayani's camp without orders, then was destroyed during its withdrawal. 623 French and colonial troops killed — France's heaviest single defeat in Morocco.

events.body:
> The best-documented Moroccan military victory over France, and the one where the French record is most detailed — because the French army investigated its own catastrophe.

## Identification

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Date | **13 November 1914** |
| Place | El Herri, c. 15 km from Khénifra · approx. 32°51′27″N 05°37′21″W |
| Context | Zaian War (1914–1921); three months into the First World War |
| Outcome | Decisive Zaian victory |

## Forces

**French column** — Lieutenant-Colonel **René Laverdure**, commanding at Khénifra.

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| Strength | **43 officers and 1,187 men** — roughly half what Laverdure had commanded in September |
| Infantry | Six companies of Algerian and Senegalese tirailleurs; a French colonial infantry detachment |
| Cavalry | A squadron of Tunisian spahis |
| Artillery | Two batteries — 65 mm mountain guns and 75 mm field guns |
| Irregulars | Goumiers |

**Zaian forces** — **Mouha ou Hammou Zayani**, with elements of Mrabtin, Aït Harkat, Aït Ischak and Aït Ichkern.

**Strength: c. 5,000 assembled during the French withdrawal.** This is a **French estimate**, made under fire by a force being destroyed, and there is no independent verification. It also describes the *peak* of a force that accumulated during the day — the number present at the opening raid was far smaller.

## Sequence

**02:30** — Laverdure marches from Khénifra **without informing his superiors**, leaving a note stating he would annihilate Hammou's camp.

**Dawn** — Complete surprise. The column finds roughly 100 tents with most fighting men absent. Artillery bombardment, then cavalry charges clear the encampment. Tribesmen rally on a hill to the south; infantry clear it. **Two of Mouha ou Hammou's wives are taken. He escapes.**

**c. 08:30** — The French loot the camp and begin to withdraw.

**Morning** — Harassment by small parties. Then the decisive fact: **the Zaian realise how small the column is.** Word spreads; a force estimated at 5,000 assembles.

**Withdrawal** — Pressure on flanks and rear; high ground occupied for aimed fire. French artillery covers the retreat but loses effectiveness against dispersed targets in broken terrain.

**The collapse** — Laverdure detaches one company of Senegalese infantry to escort the wounded to Khénifra. Other troops see it leaving and break ranks to follow. At the crossing of the **Chbouka** river the rearguard and the artillery are surrounded and overrun; the gun crews are killed.

**The end** — The survivors form square on open ground under fire from the surrounding ridges. It does not last long. Men who ran were hunted down.

**Around noon** — The wounded, their escort of 171, and **426 able-bodied survivors** reach Khénifra just ahead of the pursuit.

## Casualties

**French — well documented, from French returns:**

| Category | Killed |
|---|---|
| Algerian / Tunisian tirailleurs | 218 |
| French soldiers | 210 |
| French officers | 33 |
| Senegalese tirailleurs | 125 |
| Moroccan goumiers | 37 |
| **Total killed** | **623** |
| Wounded | 176 (171 other ranks, 5 officers) |

Roughly **65% of the column killed or wounded**. Officer losses around 90% killed or wounded — only four officers came out unhurt, all cavalry.

**Material lost:** 4 machine guns, 630 small arms, 62 horses, 56 mules, **all the artillery**, camping equipment and personal effects.

**Zaian — "at least 182 killed".**

**This figure must be handled with care.** It is a battlefield count made by the losing side, of dead left on ground the victors held. It is almost certainly a floor, not a total. The 1991 Moroccan monument at El Herri also gives 182 — which means the Moroccan commemorative figure derives from the French count rather than corroborating it.

> **Evidence note.** The monument is not a source. The 1991 obelisk lists 182 Moroccan dead, states **700** French dead (against the French return of 623), and dates the battle to **1912**. Two of its three figures are wrong. Commemoration and documentation are different things and this is a clean illustration of the difference.

## The three narratives

## Consequences

**Immediate.** Khénifra invested. Henrys sent relief — Colonel **Garnier-Duplessix**'s *groupe mobile* arrived 16 November, Henrys himself on 18 November. By month's end the garrison stood at c. 7,000, a record. Show-of-force expeditions on 19–20 November.

**The exchange.** Mouha ou Hammou took Laverdure's body and those of six officers as trophies, and later **exchanged them for his two captured wives**. A negotiated exchange between belligerents — not the behaviour of the  of French administrative vocabulary, and a detail worth keeping for exactly that reason.

**Political.** Hammou displayed the captured weapons to neighbouring tribes; recruitment rose sharply. The demonstration that France could be beaten was worth more than the four machine guns.

**Strategic.** Henrys abandoned negotiation for *"submit or starve"* — blockade, crop denial and economic strangulation rather than pursuit. By 1917 a military road through the Middle Atlas constrained Zaian movement. The war ground on for seven more years.

**Metropolitan.** The disaster influenced French thinking about how many troops Morocco could safely release to the Western Front. The Zaian war is therefore part of the history of the First World War, not a colonial footnote to it.

## Unresolved questions

1. **Actual Zaian losses.** Probably unrecoverable. Any Amazigh oral-tradition material bearing on it would be the only possible counter-source.
2. **Laverdure's motive.** Ambition is the French verdict, delivered about a man who could not answer. Was there intelligence — a report that Hammou was personally in the camp — that made the raid look justified? The Khénifra intelligence file for early November 1914 would show it.
3. **The command chain.** How much did Henrys know of Laverdure's intentions? The correspondence between Khénifra and the regional command in the preceding fortnight is the test.
4. **Zaian decision-making.** Was the counter-attack directed by Hammou or an accumulation of local initiative? The French account implies emergent mass action. No Zaian source has been used.

## Archival research plan

| Holding | What to request |
|---|---|
| **SHD, Vincennes — sous-série GR 3H (Maroc)** | Operations files, Middle Atlas / Tadla, Nov 1914; the Commandement Supérieur series (**3H 314–752** per the SHD guide, structured 1st–4th bureaux with Tadla and Meknes geographic subdivisions); Bureau des Affaires Indigènes political reports, Khénifra |
| **SHD — série N** | Ministerial cabinet telegrams on Morocco (**5N 39–64** per the SHD guide) — the Lyautey–Millerand exchange should be traceable here |
| **Archives diplomatiques, Nantes** | *Protectorat Maroc*, Résidence Générale, political correspondence Nov–Dec 1914 |
| **ANOM** | Colonial administration material and personnel dossiers |

The series designations above are taken from the SHD's own published guide to its Morocco holdings and are catalogue-verified at series level only.

## Sources

See the **Sources** database. Principal secondary works bearing directly on this battle: Gershovich, *French Military Rule in Morocco* (2005); Hoisington, *Lyautey and the French Conquest of Morocco* (1995); Windrow, *Our Friends Beneath the Sands* (2010); Bimberg, *The Moroccan Goums* (1999); Burke, "Moroccan Resistance, Pan-Islam and German War Strategy, 1914–1918", *Francia* 3 (1975).
