sources.covers: **The single most important Moroccan-authored source identified so far.** The first comprehensive *national* history of Morocco rather than a dynastic chronicle, running from the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb to the reign of Abdelaziz in 1894 — i.e. a contemporaneous Moroccan account of the whole of Phase II. Leví-Provençal noted it was the first Moroccan historical work to cite non-Muslim European sources; Gibb called it the 'last worthy representative' of traditional Arabic historiography.

sources.title: كتاب الاستقصا — Arabic text, al-Maktaba al-Shamela
sources.author: Ahmad ibn Khalid al-Nasiri; edition of Ja'far al-Nasiri and Muhammad al-Nasiri
sources.date: chronicle completed 1894; this edition Dar al-Kitab, Casablanca
sources.archivalReference: Shamela book ID 6627. Fully browsable by volume, chapter and printed page number. The Shamela instance indexes three volumes running from the Islamic conquest through the Saadian period into the seventeenth century.
sources.biasNotes: The Moroccan author's own words, in Arabic, without a French translator between the reader and the text. His commitments — sharifian legitimacy, the propriety of the Makhzen order — are legible and declared. **A separate 8-part Moroccan scholarly edition exists**, annotated by Ahmad al-Nasiri with publication supervised by **Mohamed Hajji, Ibrahim Boutaleb and Ahmed Toufiq**, recorded in the National Library of Israel catalogue (record seen in search results; the catalogue page itself returned 403 and was not retrieved). That edition, not this one, is the scholarly standard.
sources.covers: **The Arabic text is online and free.** The Shamela instance appears to end with the Saadians; the Alaouite and nineteenth-century volumes — the ones that matter most for Phase II — were not visible in its index and must be located separately. A separate Arabic printing of 1906, 427pp, is on Internet Archive as `kitabelistiqali01salgoog`.

sources.title: Les origines de la guerre du Rif
sources.author: Germain Ayache
sources.publisher: Publications de la Sorbonne (série internationale no. 19) and Société Marocaine des Éditeurs Réunis, Rabat. 374 pp.
sources.archivalReference: Full text on Internet Archive, identifier `lesoriginesdelaguerredurifgermainayache`.
sources.biasNotes: **The founding work of a Moroccan national school of history.** Ayache — a Moroccan Jewish historian who taught in Rabat — wrote deliberately against colonial historiography, and is described in the literature as constituting a historical school in his own right. He has a position: that Moroccan society had its own political logic which colonial accounts systematically failed to see. That position is an argument, not a neutral vantage, and should be read as one.
sources.covers: **The single most important secondary work for the Rif war from a Moroccan vantage**, and the counterpart to Balfour's *Deadly Embrace*, which reads the same war from Spain. Reading the two against each other is the obvious next step for Phase V. **Freely readable now.** The book's specific argument has not yet been extracted — the metadata page carries no summary and the full text was too large to retrieve in this session.

sources.title: Reconsidering the Rif Revolt (1958–1959)
sources.author: Nabil Mouline
sources.archivalReference: n/a — essay format; underlying sources not itemised in the accessible text.
sources.biasNotes: A short public-facing essay by a serious historian of Moroccan political power; the argument is careful but the evidentiary apparatus is not exposed, so figures taken from it should be treated as reported rather than documented.
sources.covers: The 1958–59 Rif revolt: causes in post-independence economic collapse and elite capture by French-zone Istiqlal figures; Mohammed Sallam Ameziane as director; c. 20,000 troops deployed, described as **four-fifths of the royal army**; Prince Moulay Hassan directing, Oufkir on the ground; c. 1,000 soldiers killed and **the massacre of 400 inhabitants at Beni Hadifa**; and Hassan II's 1984 remark to northern Moroccans that they 'have previously known the violence of the crown prince; it will be best for them not to know that of the king's.'

sources.title: Archives Marocaines (series)
sources.author: Mission scientifique du Maroc
sources.archivalReference: Volumes verified present on Internet Archive include I (1905), VI (1906), IX (1906), XIV (1908), XV (1909), XIX (1913, *Dawhat al-Nāshir* of Ibn ʿAskar), XX (1913, *Le Gharb*), XXI (1913), XXVII (1927, *Confréries religieuses au Maroc*), XXXIV (1917).
sources.biasNotes: **The archetype of colonial knowledge production**: French scholars translating and publishing the Moroccan textual tradition in the years the Protectorate was being established, in order to govern it. Its translations are usable; its framing and its selection are evidence about France, not about Morocco. Read exactly as the Bureau des Affaires Indigènes ethnography is read.
sources.covers: French translations of Moroccan chronicles, biographical dictionaries, hagiographies and regional monographs — including al-Nasiri's *al-Istiqsā*. **Freely readable on Internet Archive**, which makes it the most accessible route to Moroccan textual sources currently identified.

sources.title: Bataille Elhri (digitised document)
sources.author: Author not stated in the item metadata
sources.archivalReference: Internet Archive identifier `bataille.-elhri`. 14.3 MB, scanned 600 DPI with OCR.
sources.biasNotes: **Authorship not established.** An unattributed scanned French-language text; until the author and publication are identified it cannot be tiered above SECONDARY, and any figure taken from it must be cross-checked. Flagged here so that a later researcher does not mistake a digitised object for a documented one.
sources.covers: The battle of 13 November 1914 at El Herri, 15 km from Khénifra, in Zaian territory. Located during the Session 3 sweep of Internet Archive; **not yet read in full.**

sources.title: Cahiers des Documents Historiques de la Résistance et de la Libération
sources.author: Haut Commissariat aux Anciens Résistants et Anciens Membres de l'Armée de Libération (HCAR)
sources.date: series ongoing; the body in its current form dates from 11 January 2017
sources.archivalReference: Thematic *cahiers*, each on a single topic. Verified contents include a cahier on **the Battle of El Herri, 13 November 1914**; **Moha ou Hammou Zayani**; **Zaïd Ou Hmad** (resistance leader, 1934–1936); Sultan Sidi Mohammed ben Youssef; and the Manifesto of Independence of 11 January 1944.
sources.biasNotes: **A Moroccan state body publishing the documentary record of the resistance — and therefore an official national memory project, not a neutral archive.** Its remit is to honour resisters and members of the Liberation Army; it selects accordingly. Read it exactly as the Résidence Générale files are read: for what it records, not for what it concludes. Note also that a body founded to commemorate resistance has an institutional interest in the resistance being continuous and national, which is precisely one of the contested points in this workspace.
sources.covers: **The first Moroccan-side documentary treatment of El Herri identified in this project** — the workspace's flagship event, previously reconstructed entirely from French returns. Also the route to **Zaïd Ou Hmad**, whose dates of 1934–1936 confirm that armed resistance continued after the official end of 'pacification'. Coverage runs c. 1914–1954.

sources.title: FRUS, Conferences at Washington and Casablanca 1941–1943, Document 376 — Roosevelt dinner party, 22 January 1943
sources.author: US Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.publisher: Foreign Relations of the United States
sources.archivalReference: FRUS, The Conferences at Washington, 1941–1942, and Casablanca, 1943, Document 376. Section: Friday, January 22, 1943 (ch9subch9).
sources.biasNotes: **The crucial fact about this document is what it is.** It is an *editorial note*, not a memorandum of conversation — which means the US government's own official documentary series states, in effect, that **no single official record of the Anfa dinner exists.** FRUS reconstructs it from Hopkins's notes, McCrea's sketch, Roosevelt's later press conference, and the memoirs of Elliott Roosevelt, Kenneth Pendar and Robert Murphy. Three of those five are memoirs.
sources.covers: Attendance confirmed: the Sultan, his Grand Vizier, his Chief of Protocol, the Crown Prince, Churchill, **General Noguès** (Resident-General of Morocco) and Patton. Topics: Morocco's post-war economic development, possible American participation in it, and 'the colonial question as it applied to Morocco'. The note states Roosevelt expressed sympathy with Morocco's aspirations for independence. **It also records that Noguès had difficulty hearing the President's private conversation with the Sultan** — i.e. the Resident-General was present but excluded from the substance.

sources.title: Hespéris-Tamuda
sources.author: Faculté des Lettres et des Sciences Humaines, Université Mohammed V, Rabat
sources.date: Hespéris founded 1921; merged with the Spanish-language *Tamuda* in 1960; Arabic articles from 1991
sources.archivalReference: Archive organised by decade, 1921–1929 through 2020–2025. Back runs also on Internet Archive (identifier `HespresTamuda`, arranged by year).
sources.biasNotes: **Its own history is the history of Moroccan historiography.** *Hespéris* was founded in 1921 as the organ of the French Institut des Hautes Études Marocaines — colonial scholarship in the service of the Protectorate. *Tamuda* was its Spanish-zone counterpart. Their 1960 merger under a Moroccan university, and the appearance of Arabic articles only from 1991, tracks the slow decolonisation of the field with unusual precision. **Volumes must therefore be dated before they are weighed.**
sources.covers: The principal scholarly journal of Moroccan history for a century, in four languages. Indexed in Web of Science (ESCI, 2016) and Scopus (2024). **The obvious place to find Moroccan scholarship on every disputed point in this workspace.**

sources.title: Les origines sociales et culturelles du nationalisme marocain, 1830–1912
sources.author: Abdallah Laroui
sources.archivalReference: n/a — monograph, originally his doctoral thesis.
sources.biasNotes: Laroui's scholarship is explicitly guided by a Marxist reading of history and a radical critique of culture, language and tradition. **He is the most influential Moroccan critic of colonial and orientalist historiography**, and his critique is itself a theoretical commitment rather than a neutral corrective.
sources.covers: **Exactly the period this workspace calls Phase II — 1830 to 1912 — written by a Moroccan historian asking where Moroccan nationalism came from.** Directly relevant to the workspace's central causal argument about fiscal capture, the protection system and the collapse of Makhzen authority. Laroui (b. 1933, Azemmour; taught at Mohammed V, Rabat) also wrote *L'Histoire du Maghreb: un essai de synthèse* (1970) and *Le Maroc et Hassan II: un témoignage* (2005).

sources.title: Les sources inédites de l'histoire du Maroc de 1530 à 1845
sources.author: Henry, comte de Castries (1850–1927); continued by Pierre de Cenival and Philippe de Cossé-Brissac
sources.archivalReference: Series organised by holding country: *Archives et bibliothèques de France*, *d'Angleterre*, *d'Espagne*, *des Pays-Bas*, *du Portugal*. Multiple tomes per series. Volumes verified present on Gallica (Pays-Bas t.1–6; Angleterre série 1 t.1–2; France t.1) and on Internet Archive.
sources.biasNotes: A French colonial-era scholarly enterprise, begun in 1905 — the year of the Tangier crisis — and continued through the Protectorate. **Selecting and publishing the European documentary record of Morocco was itself part of establishing a European claim to know the country.** But the documents reproduced are transcribed in the original, which makes the collection usable against the intentions of its editors.
sources.covers: **The entry point to Phase I and early Phase II, which this workspace had left entirely empty.** Diplomatic and commercial documents on Morocco, 1530–1845, drawn from five European national archives and published in the original languages with French apparatus. Freely readable on Gallica and Internet Archive.

sources.title: Wandering Minstrels and Epic Poetry from Morocco's Berber Highlands
sources.author: Michael Peyron
sources.archivalReference: Fieldwork 2005–2007; earlier collections 1974–1988. Collaborators named: **Arsène Roux, Fatima Kadiri, Rkia Mountassir, Jeanine Drouin**.
sources.biasNotes: A European scholar of Middle Atlas Amazigh tradition, working with Moroccan collaborators. The corpus is oral and was collected decades after the events it describes; it is strong evidence of experience and community memory, and weak evidence of chronology and number — the workspace's standing rule for oral tradition applies unchanged.
sources.covers: The Amazigh counter-archive this project has repeatedly flagged as missing. Genres: ***tamdyazt*** and ***tayffart***, ballads of forty couplets or more, performed by travelling bards (***imdyazn***) under a *ššix*, with fiddle, tambourine and the reed-flute player (*bu wɣanim*) who doubled as scout and clown. **A resistance-poetry corpus covering the anti-French campaigns of 1908–1936 exists and has been collected.** Named poets include **Rwisha** (Khenifra, active c. 1984), **Hmad Waqqa** (Ayt Yahya) and the poetess **Tawkhettalt** of Tizi n-Isly. The most celebrated ballads commemorate the **Battle of Tazigzawt (1932)**, where c. 1,000 fighters faced two French divisions.

archives.fonds: Fondo África → Alta Comisaría de España en Marruecos, 4,990 cajas, 1750–1979 (classification 1.2.5.1, Órganos Centrales). Catalogued in PARES.
archives.holdings: The administrative record of the Spanish protectorate: political files, intelligence, the northern parties, the Khalifate at Tetouan.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The Rif war; northern nationalism and how far Spain sponsored it; Abd el-Krim's own official output before 1915; the Jebala and Raisuni.
archives.access: Reading room; PARES catalogue online.

archives.fonds: GR 3H — Maroc, c. 3,000 articles, 1877–1960 (item inventory 1836–1963). Commandement Supérieur 3H 314–752. Goums 3H 2375–2711. Ministerial telegrams in série N at 5N 39–64. Marine series for the 1907 bombardment.
archives.holdings: The French military and Affaires Indigènes record: operations, intelligence, tribal political reports, personnel.
archives.whatItCanSettle: El Herri and the Khénifra command chain; the 1920 Zaian submission terms; the 'submit or starve' blockade; Bougafer 1933; Franco-Spanish liaison in 1925–26 and the chemical-weapons question on the French side.
archives.access: Reading room, Vincennes. Published inventories.

archives.fonds: FO 413 — Confidential Print Morocco and North West Africa, 1839–1969, 150 volumes, open (catalogue-verified; covers Morocco throughout, extended to Algeria and Tunisia from 1952). FO 174 — Consulate, Tangier. FO 99 — Morocco general correspondence (pre-1906 series). FO 371 — political departments from 1906. Also Admiralty and War Office series.
archives.holdings: British consular, diplomatic and intelligence reporting on Morocco. Britain was the third party in Morocco until it traded its position away in the 1904 Entente, and it kept reporting afterwards.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The independent check on almost every Franco-Spanish claim in this workspace. FO 413 in particular is a curated, printed, chronological digest of British reporting on Morocco across 130 years — the single most efficient entry point to third-party evidence on Casablanca 1907, Annual 1921, the Rif Republic, the Maclean ransom and the 1953 deposition. Confidential Print includes the Foreign Office's own 'descriptions of leading personalities' — i.e. British pen-portraits of the same men French and Spanish intelligence were profiling, which allows direct comparison of three states' assessments of one person.
archives.access: Free reader's ticket; Discovery catalogue online. Some series digitised.

archives.city: Rabat — Avenue Ibn Battouta, near Bab Rouah
archives.fonds: Fonds Protectorat, organised by Protectorate office; cartons with variable levels of description. Pre- and post-Protectorate material also held.
archives.holdings: Roughly 40% of the colonial administrative archive that remained in Morocco at independence — the other 60% went to France. Administrative files, colonial economy, public works.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The Moroccan-held share of the Protectorate record. Crucially, it is the likeliest home in Morocco of the Arabic instrument of the Treaty of Fez and of the 1953 ben Arafa bay'a.
archives.access: Mon-Fri 09:00-16:00, closed August and government holidays. Three-day temporary permit; reader card requires two passport photos, a letter of attestation and ID. Doctoral students c. 100 MAD. Photography permitted free with an authorisation slip. Not wheelchair accessible.

archives.fonds: Weltkrieg files — WK Nr. 11 series cited by Odile Moreau for the Morocco operation. Pre-war Marokko files for the 1905 and 1911 crises.
archives.holdings: German diplomatic and subversion records: the Tangier crisis of 1905, the Agadir crisis of 1911 and the Franco-German convention of 4 November 1911, and the wartime Madrid channel financing and arming Moroccan resistance.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The financing figures currently repeated on thin authority — the '600,000 pesetas per month' and '300,000 marks'. The terms Moulay Abdelhafid actually demanded in Barcelona in 1915. And Hugo Stoltzenberg's chemical supply chain to Spain.
archives.access: Reading room, Berlin.

archives.institution: US National Archives (NARA) — RG 84, Foreign Service Posts
archives.fonds: RG 84 — Records of the Foreign Service Posts. Diplomatic posts: Morocco, 1905–1957. Consular posts: Morocco, 1795–1957. Also Spanish Morocco, 1942–1944.
archives.holdings: Post-level correspondence of the American Legation at Tangier and the consulates. The 1795 start date reflects the Moroccan-American treaty of 1786 — the oldest unbroken US treaty relationship.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The Perdicaris affair of 1904 from the American side; the Anfa conference and its aftermath; American reporting on the nationalist movement, which was courted by Istiqlal precisely because Washington was not a colonial power in Morocco. The Spanish Morocco series (1942–44) is a rare American window on the Spanish zone.
archives.access: Public. Some visa and personnel files require State Department consultation.

archives.fonds: HR.SYS. (Hariciye Siyasi — Foreign Ministry political). DH.KMS. (Interior, Kalem-i Mahsus). DH.MKT. (Interior correspondence). BEO (Bab-ı Ali Evrak Odası). İ.HB. (İrade Harbiye).
archives.holdings: The Ottoman record of the Teşkilât-ı Mahsusa operation in Morocco: officer despatches, Enver Pasha's directives, Madrid legation traffic, negotiations with Moulay Abdelhafid.
archives.whatItCanSettle: This is the workspace's first source of document-level references. Named scholars cite specifically: HR.SYS. 2392/2, 2393/1, 2393/2, 2393/4, D.2109 G.10, D.2392 G.5, D.2393 G.1-3; DH.KMS. 29-28; DH.MKT. 2885-31; BEO 1993-149432 and 4135-310078. These would establish the Ottoman-Moroccan relationship independently of both French and German reporting.
archives.access: Reading room in Istanbul; catalogue searchable on site. The 2013 move to the new building disrupted some access.

archives.fonds: Digitised books, periodicals, press, maps, photographs.
archives.holdings: The French press day by day — Le Temps, L'Illustration, Le Petit Journal — plus colonial-era monographs, the Archives berbères, Bulletin Officiel, and Protectorate ethnography.
archives.whatItCanSettle: Contemporary French framing of Casablanca 1907, El Herri 1914 and the Rif war, as published rather than as later rationalised. Also the Affaires Indigènes scholarly corpus — the richest surviving description of rural Moroccan society, produced in order to govern it.
archives.access: Free and fully online.

archives.fonds: Official Makhzen correspondence. Published document series al-Wathā'iq ('The Archives'), issued from 1976.
archives.holdings: Makhzen correspondence with a focus on pre-colonial Moroccan international relations — i.e. the Moroccan state's own diplomatic record.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The single largest gap in this workspace. Whether Moroccan sovereignty over the Sahara was asserted before or in reaction to European encroachment; the Makhzen's own account of the treaties of 1844, 1860, 1880 and 1906. The published al-Wathā'iq volumes are the accessible entry point and require no reading-room access.
archives.access: Restricted; a public electronic portal has been announced but not confirmed as live. The published volumes circulate in research libraries.

archives.institution: Hemeroteca Digital — Biblioteca Nacional de España
archives.fonds: Digitised Spanish newspapers and periodicals.
archives.holdings: The Spanish press, day by day — including the coverage of the 1909 Melilla campaign that produced the Semana Trágica, and of Annual in 1921.
archives.whatItCanSettle: How the disasters were reported in real time before the official accounts were settled; the political construction of the responsibilities crisis; the range of casualty figures in circulation in 1921 as against those fixed later.
archives.access: Free and fully online.

archives.institution: Foreign Relations of the United States (FRUS)
archives.city: Published — Office of the Historian, Department of State
archives.fonds: Annual and conference volumes. The Conferences at Washington and Casablanca, 1941–1943 is the relevant conference volume for Anfa.
archives.coveringDates: Nineteenth century to the recent past
archives.holdings: The official published documentary record of US foreign policy: cables, memoranda of conversation, position papers.
archives.whatItCanSettle: Anfa, 22 January 1943. This workspace previously recorded 'what Roosevelt said' as unknown. Stenner (2014) works from State Department records, cables, and photographs of Roosevelt's letters to the sultan, and concludes Roosevelt did make supportive statements which the US then denied. FRUS is where to check that directly.
archives.access: Free and fully online.

archives.fonds: Colonial administration and personnel; Algerian series bearing on the Moroccan frontier and on Abd el-Kader's descendants.
archives.holdings: The French colonial administrative record, including Algeria — which matters because the Moroccan frontier, the Touat question and the Abd el-Kader family thread all run through Algiers.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The Algerian-Moroccan frontier disputes; the Touat annexation of 1901; the surveillance of Emir Abd el-Malek, whose family France had exiled from Algeria.
archives.access: Reading room; substantial online finding aids and some digitised material.

archives.institution: League of Nations Archives / UN Geneva
archives.fonds: League of Nations Secretariat files; mandates and petitions series; press cuttings.
archives.holdings: Petitions, correspondence and press material relating to colonial North Africa. Shakib Arslan operated from Geneva and used the League's environment to internationalise the 1930 Berber dahir campaign.
archives.whatItCanSettle: How the Moroccan nationalist case was made internationally before 1945; Arslan's networks; the reception of the dahir campaign outside Morocco. Morocco was a protectorate, not a mandate, so it is not in the mandates system — but the Geneva milieu is where its case was argued.
archives.access: Reading room; substantial digitisation under the Total Digital Access project.

archives.institution: Tangier American Legation Institute for Moroccan Studies (TALIM)
archives.fonds: Legation building archive, library and museum collections.
archives.holdings: The oldest US diplomatic property abroad, gifted by Sultan Moulay Suleiman. Material on the American presence at Tangier, the Perdicaris affair, and the international zone.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The Perdicaris affair from the legation's own records — minister Samuel Gummere was the man on the spot for the 'Perdicaris alive or Raisuli dead' episode. Also the social history of the Tangier international zone.
archives.access: Museum and research library, Tangier.

archives.institution: Instance Équité et Réconciliation (IER) — final report and archive
archives.fonds: Final report (2005–06), testimony records, reparations files. Related holdings at the Conseil National des Droits de l'Homme.
archives.holdings: The Moroccan state's own investigation into the Years of Lead: disappearances, arbitrary detention, deaths in custody, and the repression of the Rif in 1958–59 and of the 1965, 1981 and 1984 risings.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The strongest available OFFICIAL source for Phase IX — a state documenting its own violence. Use it as a floor, not a ceiling: it was a negotiated process that named few individuals and did not pursue criminal accountability, and Human Rights Watch published a critical assessment in 2005.
archives.access: Report published and widely available; underlying testimony records restricted.

archives.fonds: Alaouite dynastic records
archives.holdings: ʿAlawite dynasty records, including correspondence between the sultan and his governors — precisely the material that would show how the Makhzen actually managed tribes and qaids.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The nature of the appointments that this workspace treats as disputed: Mouha ou Hammou's qaid commission, Ma al-'Aynayn's Saharan khalifate, the terms on which sultans dealt with tribal power. The conditional bay'a of 1908 may also be here.
archives.access: Palace library; access restricted and by permission.

archives.institution: Archives diplomatiques — La Courneuve and Nantes
archives.fonds: Correspondance politique / Maroc; Traités; at Nantes, Protectorat Maroc — Résidence Générale, Direction des Affaires Indigènes, and the post archives for Tangier and the consulates.
archives.holdings: French diplomatic correspondence and the civil administration of the Protectorate, as distinct from its military record.
archives.whatItCanSettle: Regnault's reporting of 29–31 March 1912; the Résidence–Paris correspondence of May–August 1953; the Algeciras and 1904 loan files; the signed French instrument of the Treaty of Fez.
archives.access: Reading rooms; finding aids published online as PDFs.

archives.fonds: Digitised out-of-copyright monographs and periodicals.
archives.holdings: Contemporary French and English works on Morocco. Confirmed present: Ch. René-Leclerc / Georges type works (La France au Maroc), Chérif Ouazzani-era material, Sségonzac's Au cœur de l'Atlas, Le Maroc artistique, a Moulay Youssef and Lyautey item dated 1912, and an item indexed as 'bataille elhri'.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The workable substitute for Gallica when its search fails. These are PRIMARY_CONTEMPORARY texts, readable now, at no cost. The next research session should exploit this before anything else.
archives.access: Free and fully online.

archives.institution: Archivio Storico Diplomatico — Ministero degli Affari Esteri
archives.fonds: Serie politica; Documenti diplomatici italiani. Also Archivio Centrale dello Stato, Ministero delle Colonie, Trattati ed accordi internazionali in materia coloniale.
archives.holdings: Italian diplomatic correspondence bearing on the North African settlement.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The Franco-Italian accords of 1900–1902, in which France conceded Italian claims in Tripolitania in exchange for Italian acquiescence in Morocco. Morocco was traded for Libya in a bilateral bargain no Moroccan participated in — the same mechanism as the 1904 Entente and the 1911 Franco-German convention, and the least examined of the three. Italy also supplied military instructors and assisted at Dar al-Makina.
archives.access: Reading room, Rome; the Documenti diplomatici italiani series is published.

archives.institution: Bibliothèque Nationale du Royaume du Maroc (BNRM)
archives.fonds: Manuscripts; historical periodicals; digitised collections
archives.holdings: Large Arabic manuscript collections and historical periodicals, including the nationalist and Protectorate-era press.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The Moroccan press record of the nationalist period; the Arabic textual tradition; possibly Ma al-'Aynayn's own writings, which this workspace currently substitutes European reports for.
archives.access: Public library with an online catalogue — unusually, better catalogued online than Archives du Maroc.

archives.institution: Institut Royal de la Culture Amazighe (IRCAM)
archives.fonds: Publications programme and the journal Asinag. Collection of oral literature, lexicography and Amazigh history.
archives.coveringDates: Institute created 2001; collections cover the oral tradition generally
archives.holdings: Amazigh language, literature and cultural documentation, including collected oral material.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The Amazigh counter-archive. This workspace has flagged from the first session that the Middle Atlas and Rif wars have no Moroccan-side written record and that oral tradition is the only alternative. IRCAM is the institution that collects it.
archives.access: Public institute; publications catalogue online. The site could not be retrieved in Session 4 — SSL certificate failure — so holdings are recorded from search results rather than from the institute's own description.

archives.institution: Association Marocaine pour la Recherche Historique (AMRH)
archives.fonds: Learned society; publications and communiqués on Moroccan historical research.
archives.holdings: Not a repository — a professional body of Moroccan historians.
archives.whatItCanSettle: Who currently works on what in Moroccan historiography, and where the live scholarly disputes sit. A directory rather than a source.
archives.access: Public website.

archives.fonds: Journal archive by decade, 1921–2025. Predecessors: Hespéris (from 1921, Institut des Hautes Études Marocaines) and Tamuda (Spanish zone), merged 1960.
archives.holdings: A century of scholarship on Moroccan history in Arabic, French, Spanish and English. Arabic articles from 1991.
archives.whatItCanSettle: Moroccan academic positions on every disputed point in this workspace. And, read chronologically, the journal is itself evidence — the shift from a French colonial institute in 1921 to a Moroccan university publishing in Arabic from 1991 is a measurable record of who was permitted to write Moroccan history.
archives.access: Journal website with archives by decade; back runs also on Internet Archive.

archives.fonds: Digital library of Arabic texts, browsable by book, volume, chapter and printed page.
archives.holdings: Includes al-Nasiri's *Kitāb al-Istiqsā* at book ID 6627, in the Dar al-Kitab (Casablanca) edition of Ja'far and Muhammad al-Nasiri.
archives.whatItCanSettle: Direct access to the Arabic text of the major Moroccan chronicle, free, with printed-page concordance. The practical answer to the workspace's oldest structural weakness — no French translator standing between the reader and a Moroccan source.
archives.access: Free and fully online.

archives.institution: Haut Commissariat aux Anciens Résistants et Anciens Membres de l'Armée de Libération (HCAR)
archives.fonds: Cahiers des Documents Historiques de la Résistance et de la Libération — thematic volumes. Verified subjects include the Battle of El Herri (13 Nov 1914), Moha ou Hammou Zayani, Zaïd Ou Hmad (1934–1936), Sidi Mohammed ben Youssef, and the Manifesto of 11 January 1944.
archives.holdings: Documentation and testimony on the armed resistance and the Armée de Libération, collected and published by a Moroccan government body. Also runs study days and testimony-collection programmes.
archives.whatItCanSettle: The Moroccan-side account of El Herri — the workspace's flagship event, until now reconstructed entirely from French casualty returns. Also the only institutional route to the testimony of surviving resisters and their families, and to Zaïd Ou Hmad, whose 1934–1936 activity contradicts the tidy French date for the end of 'pacification'.
archives.access: Government body with a public website; some cahiers published as PDFs. On-site consultation conditions not established.

relationships.label: Stoltzenberg → supplied chemical weapons capability to → Spain against the Rif
relationships.evidence: Approach of 20 Aug 1921 for mustard gas in breach of Versailles; first delivery 1923; later Spanish nationality and involvement in building La Marañosa. Documented in Kunz & Müller (1990) and Balfour (2002).

relationships.label: Ba Ahmed → regent for → Moulay Abdelaziz
relationships.evidence: Effective ruler of Morocco for six years; the sultan was systematically excluded from government until Ba Ahmed's death in 1900.

relationships.label: Hassan I → appointed → Ma al-'Aynayn as khalifa of the Sahara
relationships.evidence: A dahir appointing him representative over Saharan territories. The date determines whether the act preceded or responded to Spanish occupation at Dakhla — which is the crux of the modern territorial argument.

relationships.label: Lyautey → obtained the abdication of → Moulay Abdelhafid
relationships.evidence: Abdication secured against a large pension; Moulay Youssef installed in his place, chosen for having no independent base.

relationships.label: Poeymirau → received the submission of → the sons of Mouha ou Hammou
relationships.evidence: Hassan and Amharoq submitted, followed by c. 3,000 tents. The claim that they did so on their father's advice is a single-source assertion. The terms of the submission have not been located.

relationships.label: Franco → launched the 1936 coup from → Morocco
relationships.evidence: Career made in the Rif war; Legion commander at the Alhucemas landing 1925; airlifted the Army of Africa, Legion and Moroccan Regulares, to the peninsula. Self-referential entry recording the fact that the Spanish Civil War began in Morocco.

relationships.label: Ba Ahmed → concealed the death of → Hassan I
relationships.evidence: Chamberlain and grand vizier; concealed the sultan's death on 9 June 1894 while the column was in unsecured country, continuing to issue orders in his name, then proclaimed Abdelaziz. Duration of the concealment is not established.

relationships.label: Lyautey → patron of → Thami El Glaoui
relationships.evidence: The central client relationship of the politique des grands caïds: France armed, enriched and protected him against rivals, producing authority greater than any pre-Protectorate qaid could have held.

relationships.label: Moulay Abdelhafid → captured and executed → Bou Hamara
relationships.evidence: Fact and year established; brought to Fez in a cage. The manner of execution is disputed — the widely repeated 'fed to his lions' account is poorly sourced, and shooting and public display also appear.

relationships.label: Hassan I → appointed → Mouha ou Hammou Zayani
relationships.evidence: Reference literature records the investiture as qaid of the Zaian, brokered by the Sherqawa marabout Sidi Ben Dawd, with a black cloak, sharifian infantry and artillery. Three different years appear in works of comparable authority.

relationships.label: Laverdure → fought → Mouha ou Hammou Zayani at El Herri
relationships.evidence: Column of 43 officers and 1,187 men; 623 killed including Laverdure. Marched without orders. Two of Hammou's wives captured, later exchanged for the bodies of Laverdure and six officers.

relationships.label: Oufkir → named as responsible for the abduction of → Mehdi Ben Barka
relationships.evidence: A 1967 French trial convicted two officers of kidnapping and the judge identified Oufkir as principally responsible. The witness Georges Figon, who testified that Oufkir killed Ben Barka, was later found dead. French files remain classified.

relationships.label: Moulay Abdelhafid → deposed → Moulay Abdelaziz
relationships.evidence: Proclaimed Marrakech Aug 1907; conditional bay'a of the Fez ulama Jan 1908; Abdelaziz defeated at the Battle of Marrakech 19 Aug 1908, largely by defection, and abdicated two days later.

relationships.label: Thami El Glaoui → demanded the deposition of → Mohammed V
relationships.evidence: Public declaration of loyalty to the Protectorate and demand for the sultan's removal, 19 May 1953. Reversed 25 Oct 1955; knelt in submission 8 Nov 1955 and was pardoned. Whether the initiative was his or the Residency's is unsettled.

relationships.label: Silvestre → fought → Abd el-Krim at Annual
relationships.evidence: Expediente Picasso findings on over-extension and command failure. Spanish dead given variously as 7,875 to 13,363 depending on definition. Silvestre's manner of death not established.

relationships.label: Berenguer → authorised chemical munitions against → the Rif
relationships.evidence: Telegram to War Minister Marichalar, 12 Aug 1921: he would employ such munitions 'con verdadera fruición'. Quoted by Sebastian Balfour from Spanish archives. Not verified at document level by this project. Written three days after Monte Arruit.

relationships.label: Guillaume → deposed and exiled → Mohammed V
relationships.evidence: Deposition and exile to Corsica, then Antsirabe in Madagascar, executed under his residency. Three versions of who decided — Paris, Guillaume, or El Glaoui and the notables — remain in circulation and are settleable from the Residency-Paris correspondence.

relationships.label: Regnault → negotiated the Treaty of Fez with → Moulay Abdelhafid
relationships.evidence: A negotiation session reported at around six hours on 29 March, with French troops in and around Fez; signed 30 March. Regnault's own reporting to the Quai d'Orsay would establish what pressure was applied and has not been read.

relationships.label: Raisuni → abducted → Harry Maclean
relationships.evidence: Ransomed for £20,000 paid by the British government, after Raisuni's removal from the pashalik of Tangier. Note: the date 1907 circulates and appears to be wrong.

relationships.label: Si Madani El Glaoui → engineered the accession of → Moulay Abdelhafid
relationships.evidence: Prominent among the southern notables who invited Abdelhafid, then khalifa at Marrakech, to take the throne. Became his grand vizier. His brother Thami was made pasha of Marrakech.

relationships.label: Pétain → superseded → Lyautey
relationships.evidence: Sent with overriding authority after Abd el-Krim's April 1925 offensive on the Ouergha; Lyautey resigned. Read structurally, the tache d'huile method had reached its limit against a rival state with an army.

relationships.label: Mohammed ben Arafa → installed in place of → Mohammed V
relationships.evidence: Proclaimed by an assembly of notables. Never accepted; two assassination attempts. The bay'a assembled for him, with its signatories and refusals, is a documentable map of elite alignment in 1953.

places.whyItMatters: Stone town with mosque and library founded by Ma al-'Aynayn from around 1898 — a deliberate assertion of permanence and statehood in territory European powers classified as empty. Razed by French forces in 1913. That destruction of the physical evidence of a Saharan polity is itself a documentable act with lasting political consequences.
places.tribes: Tekna, Reguibat and the Saharan confederations of the Saguia el-Hamra
places.militaryPresence: French Saharan column, 1913. Later Spanish Sahara administration.

places.whyItMatters: Political and religious capital until 1912. Al-Qarawiyyin and its ulama were the source of the conditional bay'a of 1908 and of much nationalist leadership. Site of the 1874 tanners' revolt, the 1911 siege, the Treaty of 30 March 1912, and the rising of 17 April 1912 in which the mellah was shelled and sacked. The capital was moved to Rabat immediately afterwards.
places.tribes: Urban; hinterland of the Saiss plain
places.militaryPresence: Moinier's relief column May 1911; French garrison from 1911; Dar al-Makina arsenal (1888) predates it.

places.otherNames: الرباط · Rabat · Salé across the Bou Regreg
places.whyItMatters: Made capital by Lyautey after the April 1912 rising — one of the most consequential administrative decisions of the Protectorate, displacing the inland city of the ulama in favour of a coastal, controllable seat. Site of the Résidence Générale, Prost's ville nouvelle, and the post-1956 state. Salé's Great Mosque is where the Ya Latif campaign began on 20 June 1930.
places.militaryPresence: Résidence Générale and central French command from 1912.

places.whyItMatters: Seat of Mouha ou Hammou Zayani and the Zaian confederation; occupied by Henrys in June 1914; besieged after El Herri; the French base from which Laverdure marched on 13 November 1914. Garrison reached c. 7,000 by end November 1914 — a French figure.
places.militaryPresence: French groupe mobile base 1914–1921; Bureau des Affaires Indigènes post. Its BAI political bulletins are a priority archival target.

places.otherNames: Axdir · أجدير · Alhucemas · Al Hoceima · Sp.: 'Bahía de Alhucemas'
places.whyItMatters: Abd el-Krim's home and the seat of the Rif Republic 1921–1926. Target of Silvestre's 1921 advance and of the combined Franco-Spanish amphibious landing of 8 September 1925 — an operation later studied internationally as a model for opposed landings.
places.militaryPresence: Rif Republic administrative centre; Spanish landing and occupation from September 1925.

places.whyItMatters: Spanish presidio since 1497 and the base of Spanish expansion into the eastern Rif. Its hinterland saw the 1909 campaign and the Barranco del Lobo, and the 1921 Annual collapse which left the city itself almost undefended. Abd el-Krim worked here as journalist, interpreter and qadi before 1915. Remains Spanish.
places.tribes: Guelaya, Beni Bou Ifrour, Beni Sicar and the eastern Rif tribes
places.militaryPresence: Comandancia General; the Melilla command's records are a core Spanish archival target.

places.whyItMatters: Capital of the Spanish protectorate and seat of the Khalifa nominally representing the sultan. Captured by Spain in 1860, the war that produced the Wad Ras indemnity. Centre of nationalism in the Spanish zone under Abdelkhalek Torres, and of an Arabic press largely unread in French-centred accounts.
places.militaryPresence: Alta Comisaría de España en Marruecos; the fonds of 4,990 boxes at AGA is the principal Spanish holding.

places.whyItMatters: Site of the 13 November 1914 battle: 623 French and colonial troops killed, France's heaviest single defeat in Morocco. A 1991 commemorative obelisk stands there and contains at least two factual errors — it gives 700 French dead and dates the battle to 1912.
places.tribes: Zaian, Mrabtin, Aït Harkat, Aït Ischak, Aït Ichkern
places.militaryPresence: None permanent; the site of a raid, not a post. c. 15 km from Khénifra.

groups.otherNames: Aith Waryaghar · Beni Ouriaghel · Sp.: 'Beni Urriaguel'
groups.region: Central Rif, around Ajdir and Alhucemas bay
groups.politicalPosition: The nucleus of Abd el-Krim's Rif Republic 1921–1926; the target of the 1925 Alhucemas landing and of chemical bombardment.
groups.notes: Abd el-Krim's own tribe. Hart's The Aith Waryaghar of the Moroccan Rif (1976) is the standard ethnography. Key research question: how a segmentary society with institutionalised feuding produced, within about two years, a centralised authority capable of suppressing the feud and fielding a coordinated army. That transformation — not the battles — is the real subject of the Rif war.

groups.otherNames: حزب الاستقلال · Hizb al-Istiqlal · Parti de l'Indépendance
groups.region: Fez, Rabat, Salé, Casablanca — urban and largely northern-urban in origin
groups.politicalPosition: Founded 1943–44; issued the Independence Manifesto of 11 January 1944; split in 1959 with the departure of the UNFP left.
groups.notes: Its urban, Arabophone, Fassi-notable social base is the fact most often left implicit — and it explains both its organisational strength and its distance from the rural resistance of the Middle and High Atlas and the Rif. The 1959 split producing the UNFP (Ben Barka, Bouabid, Ibrahim) is the founding division of post-independence Moroccan politics. Its rival in the French zone was Ouazzani's PDI; in the Spanish zone, Torres's Partido de Reformas Nacionales.

groups.region: High Atlas, Telouet and the Tizi n'Tichka pass
groups.politicalPosition: Backed Abdelhafid in 1907 and France from 1912; the central Moroccan instrument of the politique des grands caïds until 1955.
groups.notes: Power rested on control of the Tichka pass and the trade through it — salt, dates, minerals — then on French arms. Under the Protectorate the family held authority no pre-colonial caïd could have held, because the Makhzen counterweight had been removed. Property confiscated and the house broken politically after 1956.

groups.politicalPosition: A guich and makhzen-linked tribe of the Marrakech region; repeatedly involved in dynastic contests including the Hafidiya.
groups.notes: Stub. The guich tribes — holding land in return for military service — are an under-researched category in this workspace and they are the hinge between Makhzen fiscal-military organisation and tribal society. Others include the Oudaya, Cherarda and Bouakher. A dedicated study of the guich system is a priority.

groups.region: Western Rif and the hinterland of Tangier, Tetouan and Chefchaouen
groups.politicalPosition: Raisuni's base; a second and partly rival theatre of resistance in the Spanish zone, distinct from Abd el-Krim's Rif.
groups.notes: Arabic-speaking and religiously organised around sharifian lineages and zawiyas, in contrast to the Tarifit-speaking eastern Rif. The Jebala/Rif distinction is essential and is routinely collapsed in general accounts. Raisuni and Abd el-Krim were not allies; Rifian forces captured Raisuni in 1925.

groups.region: Atlantic plain around Casablanca and Settat
groups.politicalPosition: Site of the 30 July 1907 killings that triggered the French bombardment of Casablanca; subject of d'Amade's 1908 campaign.
groups.notes: The first region of Atlantic Morocco brought under sustained French military occupation, four years before the Protectorate. Its subsequent transformation into the agricultural and industrial hinterland of Casablanca makes it the best case study of colonial land expropriation and capitalist agriculture in Morocco — a subject this workspace has not begun.

groups.otherNames: Zaïans · Zaïanes · Zayanes (Sp.) · Izayyan · Aït Yaʿqoub and Aït Harkat (halves/sections)
groups.region: Central Middle Atlas, around Khénifra and the upper Oum er-Rbia
groups.politicalPosition: Makhzen-invested qaid under Hassan I; core of armed resistance to France 1914–1921; partial submission from June 1920.
groups.notes: French estimates give 4,000–4,200 tents under Mouha ou Hammou's authority — an estimate, not a census. The confederation assembled for specific occasions rather than operating as a standing hierarchy, which is why French strength figures swing so widely. Research gap: how decisions were taken in the Zaian jema'a. No Zaian-side written source has been used here.

groups.otherNames: Ait Atta · Aït 'Atta · Fr.: 'les Aït Atta'
groups.region: South-eastern High Atlas, Jbel Saghro, Dadès and Draa valleys, pre-Sahara
groups.politicalPosition: Among the last confederations brought under French control; held Bougafer in 1933 and ended it on negotiated terms.
groups.notes: Governed through a rotating, elected leadership system rather than hereditary chieftaincy — institutionalised constraint on any individual's power. French administrative categories, built around the caïd, handled this badly. One of the clearest cases where colonial vocabulary actively obscures Moroccan political reality. David M. Hart's ethnography is the standard reference and is itself a product of the colonial knowledge apparatus.

pages.title: bias
pages.body:
> **Standing rule: where sources disagree, the disagreement is the finding. Do not silently choose.**

## How each archive lies

Not "is biased" — *lies*, in the specific and predictable ways an institution's paperwork lies about the thing it was built to do.

### French Protectorate sources

**Systematically reliable on:** their own casualties, unit strengths, dates, movements, logistics. Armies count their own dead accurately because pensions and replacements depend on it.

**Systematically unreliable on:**

- **Enemy numbers.** Inflated when explaining defeat, deflated when claiming victory. The "c. 5,000 Zaian" at El Herri was estimated by men being destroyed.
- **Moroccan political motives.** Resistance is filed as fanaticism, banditry, feudal coercion or foreign manipulation — never as politics. A category error built into the filing system.
- **The legitimacy of Moroccan authority.** *Dissident* and *insoumis* mean "outside French authority." They are reproduced constantly as if they meant "illegitimate."
- **Civilian effects.** Blockade, crop denial and the "submit or starve" policy generate almost no documentation of their human cost, because no French institution was tasked with recording it.

**The deepest structural distortion:** the Protectorate's legitimating claim was that it *preserved* Moroccan sovereignty. Every document is written inside that fiction. It is not incidental — it is the frame.

### Spanish Protectorate sources

**Reliable on:** the internal Spanish political fight, because that fight was conducted through documents — the **Expediente Picasso** exists because Spaniards wanted to blame each other.

**Unreliable on:**

- **Their own casualties**, uniquely. The range for Annual runs 7,875 to 13,363 and it is a *Spanish* range, driven by whether Moroccan troops in Spanish service are counted.
- **Chemical weapons.** Documented in authorisation and supply; systematically undocumented in effect. No Spanish record counts who died of gas.
- **Moroccan casualties.** Essentially absent.

**Structural distortion:** Spanish sources are overwhelmingly about *Spain*. Morocco is the setting for a Spanish argument about the army, the monarchy and the nation. Moroccans appear as a problem, rarely as agents.

### Moroccan nationalist sources

**Reliable on:** the urban nationalist movement's own organisation, its internal debates, its texts.

**Unreliable on:**

- **The relationship between rural resistance and urban nationalism.** These were largely separate movements. The national narrative retrospectively unifies them.
- **Collaboration.** Personalised in **El Glaoui**, which spares the several hundred other pashas, qaids and notables who made the system work.
- **Post-1956 continuity.** The colonial security apparatus was inherited, not dismantled — **Oufkir** is the proof. This is not comfortable and is not emphasised.
- **Casualty and participation figures** in resistance episodes, which are commemorative rather than documentary. **The El Herri monument gets two of its three figures wrong.**

### Amazigh sources and oral tradition

**Reliable on:** what the affected communities remember, transmitted through *izlan* and *timdyazin* — which for the rural conquest is often the *only* surviving account from the Moroccan side.

**Unreliable on:** chronology, which oral form compresses and reorders; and numbers, which perform emphasis rather than count.

**Rule:** neither automatically true nor automatically false. Oral tradition is strong evidence of experience and weak evidence of dates. Treat it exactly as one would treat a memoir.

### British and American sources

**Value:** genuinely third-party for most of the period, and therefore the best available check on Franco-Spanish claims. FO 371 and State Department files are systematically underused in Moroccan historiography.

**Caution:** Britain had its own Moroccan policy until 1904 and its own Mediterranean interests after. Walter Harris, the most quoted British source, was a journalist writing for effect.

### German sources

**Value:** Germany had an interest in embarrassing France and Spain, which makes German reporting a useful counterweight — German estimates of Casablanca 1907 deaths run three to five times French ones. Germany was also a **participant**: it financed and armed Moroccan resistance in the First World War, and it supplied Spain's chemical weapons capability through **Hugo Stoltzenberg**.

**Caution:** for exactly the same reason. And note that after 1914 Germany is no longer a neutral observer of Morocco but a belligerent operating inside it.

### Ottoman sources — added Session 2

**Value:** the Ottoman Empire ran its own operation in Morocco from 1914 through the Teşkilât-ı Mahsusa, based in Madrid. Its officers reported to Istanbul, and they reported **inconvenient things about their German allies** — which makes the Ottoman file an unusually candid source on the whole wartime subversion effort.

**Two findings this workspace could not have obtained elsewhere:** Moulay Abdelhafid's Barcelona negotiation of 1915, and Taher Bey's observation that a large share of the notables Ottoman intelligence decorated as resistance figures were prospering under the French.

**Caution:** Ottoman reporting inflates the prospects of pan-Islamic mobilisation, because that was the premise of the operation and of the officers' own careers. Their strength figures for allied Moroccan forces should be treated exactly as French estimates of enemy strength are treated.

**Uniquely valuable feature:** these are the **only document-level archival references currently in this workspace** — real BOA strings from published scholarship, usable on a call slip.

---

## The live contradictions

| # | Question | Positions | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Casablanca 1907 deaths** | French 600–1,500; German 2,000–3,000; Moroccan higher | **Unresolvable on present evidence.** Range only |
| 2 | **Treaty of Fez: Arabic vs French text** | Moroccan legal argument says they differ in substance; no comparison performed here | **Settleable.** Highest verification priority |
| 3 | **Annual dead** | 7,875 / 8,180 / 8,668 / 13,363 | **Definitional.** State the range and the definitions |
| 4 | **Silvestre's death** | Suicide / killed / unknown | **Unknown.** Suicide is repeated, not documented |
| 5 | **Alfonso XIII's telegrams** | Alleged encouragement of Silvestre | **Alleged, never proven.** Record as allegation |
| 6 | **Zaian dead at El Herri** | French count 182; Moroccan monument repeats 182 | **A French floor, not a total.** The monument is not independent corroboration |
| 7 | **Mouha ou Hammou's death** | Killed by his son Hassan / by a party his sons had joined / in a clash with French-allied partisans | **Disputed.** Three different claims routinely collapsed into one |
| 8 | **Who decided the 1953 deposition** | Paris / Guillaume / El Glaoui and the notables | **Settleable** from Residency–Paris correspondence |
| 9 | **Bou Hamara's execution** | Fed to lions / shot / other | **Disputed.** Fact and date established; manner not |
| 10 | **Ma al-'Aynayn's status** | Makhzen agent / autonomous sovereign | **Both, shifting over time.** Any clean resolution is politically motivated |
| 11 | **The Berber dahir** | Deliberate de-Islamisation plot / extension of existing law received as a plot | **Both matter.** The perception did the historical work |
| 12 | **French chemical weapons use** | Spanish use documented; French use or acquiescence 1925–26 | **Open.** Neither assert nor dismiss |
| 13 | **Ben Barka** | Oufkir named by a French court; Dlimi, Mossad, CIA alleged | **Documents exist and are withheld.** A different category from unknown |
| 14 | **Moroccan troops in 1936 Spain** | Volunteers / famine-driven / coerced by qaids | **Under-researched and uncomfortable for everyone** |

---

## Method rules that follow

1. **Never state a single casualty figure where a range exists.** Give the range and the definitions.
2. **Never reproduce a colonial administrative label as description.** Quote it, attribute it, explain what the filing category meant.
3. **A commemorative monument is not a source.**
4. **When both sides benefit from a story, check it.** The fratricide at Azlag n'Tazemmourt is the type-case.
5. **Distinguish *unknown* from *withheld*.** Silvestre's death is unknown. Ben Barka's file is withheld. These require different language and different follow-up.
6. **Where a European report describes a Moroccan's motives, treat it as evidence about the reporter.**
7. **Never merge people with similar names.** See the open entry on "Sidi Mohamed Ben Hammou".

pages.title: cross-verification
pages.body:
> **The purpose of going global is not coverage. It is triangulation.** A dispute between France and Spain cannot be settled by France or Spain. This page maps every live dispute in the workspace to the archive of a state that had no stake in that particular quarrel.

## The principle

Moroccan history has been written overwhelmingly from the records of the two states that conquered it. Those states disagreed with each other constantly, which historians have sometimes mistaken for a form of balance. It is not. **Two interested parties disagreeing is not corroboration.**

The useful question for any claim is: *which state was watching, kept records, and had no reason to lie about this particular thing?*

| Period | Who was watching without a stake | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1830–1904 | **Britain** | Wanted a viable Morocco as a check on France; reported accurately because it needed accurate information |
| 1904–1914 | **Germany**, and Britain residually | Germany's interest was in embarrassing France, so it over-reported French abuses — but it reported them |
| 1914–1918 | **Ottoman Empire** | Running its own operation; its officers reported what they saw to Istanbul, including inconvenient things about their German allies |
| 1918–1939 | **Britain** | No claim in Morocco; watched Spain closely because of Gibraltar |
| 1940–1956 | **United States** | Not a colonial power in Morocco, courted by both the palace and the Istiqlal |
| 1956–1999 | **United States, France** | Both have documents; both are still withholding some |

## The matrix

| # | Dispute | Interested parties | **Who can settle it** | Status now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Casablanca 1907 deaths** (600–1,500 Fr. vs 2,000–3,000 Ger.) | France, Germany | **TNA FO 413 / FO 174** — British consular reporting from Tangier and Casablanca. Britain had no stake in the number | Open |
| 2 | **Treaty of Fez: Arabic vs French text** | France, Morocco | **Archives du Maroc / Hassaniya** for the Arabic; **Archives diplomatiques, *Traités*** for the French. Also FO 413, which would carry the British translation made at the time | Open — highest priority |
| 3 | **Annual dead** (7,875–13,363) | Spain only | **Expediente Picasso** is Spanish, but the range is a *Spanish* argument. **TNA FO 371** and the international press give the figures circulating before the official account settled | Open |
| 4 | **Silvestre's death** | Spain | Probably unsettleable. **Rifian oral tradition** is the only non-Spanish source, and it has not been sought | Unknown |
| 5 | **Alfonso XIII's telegrams to Silvestre** | Spain | **TNA FO 371** — the British embassy in Madrid reported the responsibilities crisis closely. Would not prove the telegrams but would show what Madrid believed at the time | Alleged |
| 6 | **Zaian dead at El Herri** | France (and a Moroccan monument copying the French figure) | **No archive can settle this.** Only Amazigh oral tradition, and it will not yield a number. Record the French floor of 182 and stop | Unresolvable |
| 7 | **Mouha ou Hammou's death** | France, Moroccan and Amazigh memory | **SHD GR 3H**, Khénifra BAI bulletins Mar–Apr 1921 — but France reported it through allied partisans, so it is not disinterested. **Ottoman/German records end in 1918**, so no third party was watching | Disputed |
| 8 | **Who decided the 1953 deposition** | France, El Glaoui's heirs, the Moroccan monarchy | **Archives diplomatiques de Nantes** (Résidence–Paris) *and* **TNA FO 371** *and* **NARA RG 84** — both Britain and the US reported the crisis and neither had a position to defend | Settleable |
| 9 | **Bou Hamara's execution** | Makhzen, European press | **FO 174 / FO 413** — British consular reporting from Fez and Tangier in 1909. The lion story circulated in the European press; British diplomatic reporting is the check on the press | Disputed |
| 10 | **Ma al-'Aynayn's appointment: 1879 or 1887** | Morocco, France, Spain, and the modern Sahara dispute | ***al-Wathā'iq*** and the **Direction des Archives Royales** — the dahir itself. This is a Moroccan document and only a Moroccan archive holds it | Settleable |
| 11 | **The Berber dahir: plot or extension** | France, Moroccan nationalism, Amazigh movement | **League of Nations / Geneva** and the Arab press — how it was understood abroad at the time, via **Shakib Arslan**. Also **FO 371** | Open |
| 12 | **French chemical weapons use 1925–26** | France, Spain | **TNA FO 371** and **A.A.-P.A.** — Britain watched the Rif war closely; Germany supplied the agents to Spain and would know who else was buying | Open |
| 13 | **Ben Barka** | France, Morocco, Israel, US | **NARA / CIA** — c. 1,800 documents acknowledged in 1976 and undisclosed. This is **withheld, not unknown** | Withheld |
| 14 | **Moroccan Regulares in 1936: volunteers or coerced** | Spain (both sides), Morocco | **TNA FO 371** and **NARA** — both watched recruitment in the Spanish zone. Also **AGA** recruitment records | Under-researched |
| 15 | **What Roosevelt said at Anfa** | US, Moroccan nationalism, France | **FRUS + State Dept records + the Roosevelt letters** | **PARTLY RESOLVED — see below** |
| 16 | **Moulay Abdelhafid's politics in exile** | France, Spain | **BOA HR.SYS.** and **A.A.-P.A. WK Nr. 11** | **RESOLVED — see below** |

---

## What the global pass actually changed

Two entries moved. Both moved because a **third state's archive** was consulted.

### 1. Moulay Abdelhafid was not politically inert in exile

**Previously:** a pensioned ex-sultan, finished after 1912; German attempts to use him as a figurehead noted vaguely and dismissed.

**Now, on Ottoman records:** in **January–February 1915 he was in Barcelona negotiating with the Ottoman officer Taher Bey** the terms on which he would return to lead a general rising against France. He demanded international recognition, **300,000 marks**, and — if it failed — *a palace in Istanbul and a salary suitable for his position*. **Enver Pasha approved support in February 1915.**

**Why neither France nor Morocco recorded this prominently.** France had no interest in publicising that the sultan who signed the Protectorate was trying to overthrow it. Moroccan nationalist historiography had no use for a would-be liberator demanding a palace as his downside protection. **It took a third archive, in a third language, held by a state that no longer exists.**

References cited by Kaya and Moreau: **BOA HR.SYS. D.2392 G.5** (the Barcelona meeting); **D.2109 G.10** (Enver's approval).

### 2. Roosevelt did make promises at Anfa — and no transcript exists, which FRUS itself says

**Session 2, on Stenner (2014):** Roosevelt made supportive statements; the US government subsequently denied them; Moroccan nationalists built the denial and the promise together into a political instrument. "Unknown" was the wrong classification.

**Session 3 — verified directly.** **FRUS, Casablanca 1943, Document 376** was consulted. It is an **editorial note, not a memorandum of conversation**: the American official series states in effect that **no single official record of the dinner exists**, and reconstructs it from Hopkins's notes, McCrea's sketch, Roosevelt's press conference, and the memoirs of Elliott Roosevelt, Pendar and Murphy.

It establishes the attendance (the Sultan, the Grand Vizier, the Chief of Protocol, the Crown Prince, Churchill, **Noguès**, Patton), the topics (post-war economic development, American participation, *"the colonial question as it applied to Morocco"*), and that Roosevelt expressed sympathy with Morocco's aspirations for independence.

**And it records that Noguès had difficulty hearing the President's private conversation with the Sultan.** The Resident-General was at the table and could not hear what was said to the man he governed. Not a transcript — but contemporaneous evidence that the conversation happened, out of French earshot, which is the point both the French denial and the nationalist claim have always turned on.

**Final status:** the substance is Established; the wording is **permanently Unknown**, and the site should say so rather than leave the question open. `Consulted directly` — the first primary source in this workspace read at document level rather than through a scholar.

---

## The uncomfortable finding

One piece of Ottoman evidence deserves separating out, because it cuts across every national narrative in this workspace.

**Taher Bey compiled a list of Moroccan notables to receive Ottoman and German decorations in April 1915.** A scholar working from the file notes that *"a remarkable part consisted of people…who achieved important positions in full harmony with the French."*

Ottoman intelligence was decorating, as resistance figures, men who were simultaneously prospering inside the Protectorate.

**This is contemporaneous, third-party, documentary evidence that for a large part of the Moroccan notability, resistance and collaboration were not alternatives but a portfolio.** It is inconvenient to the French account (which needed clean categories to administer), to the nationalist account (which needed clean categories to build a nation), and to the Amazigh account (which needs them to argue exclusion). It survives because the people who wrote it down were arguing about something else entirely.

**That is the whole case for going global.**

---

## What is still missing after this pass

| Gap | Where it would be filled |
|---|---|
| **The Moroccan state's own voice** | ***al-Wathā'iq***, published from 1976 — accessible, in print, and not yet used. **The top priority of the next session** |
| Sultan–governor correspondence | Hassaniya palace library, Rabat — restricted |
| Rifian and Zaian voices | No written archive identified. Oral tradition and family holdings |
| Women | Absent from every archive listed on this page |
| Enslaved and coerced labour | Absent likewise |
| Portuguese and Dutch early modern | Phase I is entirely unresearched; Lisbon and The Hague hold the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Moroccan record |

pages.title: synthesis
pages.body:
> **The master document. It is not a sequence of kings.** It reads Moroccan history as an interaction between the Makhzen, the tribes, the religious authorities, armed resistance, France, Spain, the nationalist parties and foreign economic interests — and it says where the evidence runs out.

## The argument in one paragraph

Morocco did not lose its independence in 1912. It lost it in instalments, mostly financial, between 1844 and 1906, and the military conquest that followed was the collection of a debt already contracted. The instrument was not primarily the army; it was the **treaty, the indemnity, the loan and the consular protection**. Once the Makhzen could not tax — because the people worth taxing were under foreign protection, and because the customs were pledged to foreign creditors — it could not pay for an army, and once it could not pay for an army it could not enforce the taxation. That loop closed decisively at Algeciras in **1906**. Everything after is consequence.

---

## I. The fiscal trap, 1844–1906

The conventional story is military: Isly 1844, Tetouan 1860, Casablanca 1907, Fez 1912. The evidence points somewhere else.

| Instrument | Date | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Anglo-Moroccan commercial treaty | 1856 | Tariff ceilings; commercial penetration |
| **Treaty of Wad Ras** | **1860** | **Indemnity mortgaging customs revenue** |
| Madrid Convention | 1880 | **Protection codified**, foreign land ownership admitted |
| French loans | from 1904 | Customs receipts pledged |
| **Act of Algeciras** | **1906** | **State Bank; customs and police under European supervision** |

The **protection system** (*ḥimāya*) is the mechanism that deserves far more attention than it gets. Consulates could place Moroccan merchants and rural notables outside Makhzen taxation and jurisdiction. Hassan I called the Madrid Conference of 1880 to curb it; the conference codified it. Abdelaziz's **tertib** — a uniform, universal agricultural tax — was the last serious attempt to escape the trap, and it failed largely because a universal tax that exempts the wealthiest is not universal and cannot be legitimated.

> **The single most valuable unanswered quantitative question in this workspace:** how many protégés were there, and what proportion of taxable wealth did they represent? The consular registers exist. **Answering this would settle the central causal argument about the fall of the Moroccan state.**

## II. What the Makhzen actually was

The colonial binary — *bled el-makhzen* (governed) versus *bled es-siba* (dissidence) — is an administrative convenience that has been mistaken for a description for a century.

The evidence in this workspace points to something else: **a system of negotiated sovereignty.** The sultan's religious authority as *Amīr al-Muʾminīn* was near-universally acknowledged. What was negotiated — continuously, sometimes violently — was taxation, appointment and jurisdiction.

Three cases make the point:

- **Mouha ou Hammou Zayani** held a Makhzen commission from Hassan I, obtained through a recognised religious broker. French reporting filed him as *insoumis*. He was not outside the Moroccan order; he occupied the position that order offered a mountain confederation.
- **Ma al-'Aynayn** was made khalifa of the Sahara in 1887 — sovereignty delegated to a religious figure with his own following, because that was how the Makhzen reached where it could not garrison.
- **The Aït Atta** rotated leadership by election. There was no caïd for France to co-opt, which is precisely why Bougafer took until 1933.

**The zawiyas are the missing layer.** Sidi Ben Dawd Sherqawi brokering Mouha ou Hammou's investiture; Ali Amhaouch supplying cross-tribal legitimacy in the Middle Atlas; Ma al-'Aynayn's Qadiriyya-Fadiliyya network holding the Sahara. Religious lineages were the connective tissue between Makhzen and tribe, and this workspace has barely touched them.

## III. How conquest actually worked

Not mainly by battle. Four techniques, in rough order of importance:

**1. Manufacturing intermediaries.** The *politique des grands caïds*. **Thami El Glaoui** is the type-case: a real pre-existing house, built by his brother **Madani**, then armed and enriched by France until it held power no pre-colonial caïd could have held — because the Makhzen counterweight had been removed. The intermediary's power depends entirely on the coloniser, which is what makes him reliable, and which is why he collapsed within weeks of France changing course in 1955.

**2. Economic strangulation.** After El Herri, Henrys abandoned pursuit for ***"submit or starve"*** — blockade, crop and pasture denial, and by 1917 a military road cutting Zaian movement. This killed far more people than the battles and **generated almost no documentation**, because no French institution was tasked with recording it.

**3. Overwhelming technical superiority at the decisive moment.** **Sidi Bou Othmane**, 6 September 1912: c. 2,000 dead against very light French losses. Machine guns and quick-firing artillery against massed cavalry. Whenever Moroccan forces accepted a set-piece engagement they were destroyed; the only Moroccan victories — El Herri, Annual — came against isolated or retreating columns.

**4. Colonised soldiers.** At El Herri, 218 Algerian/Tunisian and 125 Senegalese tirailleurs died — **55% of the French dead.** Morocco was conquered substantially by other colonised people, and it later supplied tens of thousands of Regulares to Franco's war in Spain. Neither French nor Moroccan national memory has anywhere to put this.

## IV. Two Moroccos, 1930–1934

The single most useful reframing this workspace produces.

| Same years | Urban Morocco | Rural Morocco |
|---|---|---|
| 1930 | Ya Latif campaign; the nationalist movement acquires mass form | — |
| 1933 | Party organisation, press, petitions, Geneva contacts | **Bougafer** — the Aït Atta under artillery and aircraft in the Jbel Saghro |

**These were two different struggles, in two different languages, with almost no organisational contact.** The nationalist movement was urban, Arabophone, and led by Fassi notables; the armed resistance was rural, Tamazight-speaking, and fought a war of conquest that did not end until 1934. The independence narrative constructed after 1956 unified them retrospectively.

This is the substance of the Amazigh historiographical argument, and on the evidence it is correct as a description. What it does not establish — and what should not be smuggled in with it — is that the unification was a conspiracy rather than the ordinary process by which victorious movements write their own past.

## V. Why 1953 destroyed the Protectorate

The Protectorate's entire architecture was a **legal fiction**: Morocco remained sovereign, the sultan remained sultan, *dahirs* were still signed by him. That fiction is what made the system cheap — and it made the sultan's person the one component France could not replace.

France replaced him anyway on **20 August 1953**, and discovered it could depose a sultan but could not manufacture one. **Ben Arafa** was never accepted; two attempts were made on his life; the countryside and the cities rose; the Army of Liberation formed. Within two years France restored the man it had exiled and left the country.

**The consequence that structures everything after.** Independence was negotiated *after* Mohammed V's restoration and largely on the monarchy's terms. The parties and the armed resistance had done much of the mobilising; the palace collected the sovereignty. That asymmetry explains the dismissal of the **Ibrahim** government in May 1960, the 1959 Istiqlal split and the founding of the UNFP, the suppression of the **Rif rising in 1958–59** by the army of the newly independent state, and ultimately the removal of **Ben Barka** in 1965.

## VI. Continuity across 1956

The rupture is less complete than either narrative allows.

- **Personnel.** **Oufkir** — decorated French officer, then Director-General of National Security, then Interior Minister. **Bekkay** — French officer and pasha, then first prime minister. The security apparatus of independent Morocco was staffed by men the colonial army trained.
- **Method.** The FAR suppressed the Rif in 1958–59 using techniques inherited directly from the pacification.
- **Territory.** **Allal al-Fassi's** "Greater Morocco" doctrine rests on the Hassanian-era acts documented in the Phase II dossiers. **The nineteenth-century Saharan question is the twentieth- and twenty-first-century Western Sahara question.**
- **Geography.** Three administrations, two European languages, two legal traditions and radically unequal infrastructure investment between the French and Spanish zones. The north–south divide of independent Morocco is a colonial artefact and is still visible.

## VII. What we actually know, and how

**Well established.** The chronology of treaties and campaigns. French casualties in French engagements. The institutional architecture of both protectorates. Spanish command failures at Annual, because Spain investigated itself. The authorisation and supply of Spanish chemical weapons. The sequence of the nationalist movement.

**Established but contested in interpretation.** Whether reform failed on its own terms or was destroyed by the debt and protection regimes. Whether Lyautey's respect for Moroccan institutions was principle or technique. Whether the Berber dahir was a plot or an extension received as one.

**Genuinely unknown.** Moroccan casualties in almost every engagement. The civilian cost of blockade. Makhzen finances in any year. Silvestre's death. The manner of Mouha ou Hammou's. What Roosevelt said at Anfa. Where Ben Barka is.

**Withheld rather than unknown — a different category.** French files on Ben Barka. Roughly 1,800 acknowledged CIA documents. Spanish acknowledgement of systematic chemical use, refused by parliamentary vote in 2007. **These are questions with answers that someone possesses.**

## VIII. The honest statement about this workspace

It is a **source-critical synthesis of the accessible secondary and catalogue literature, with a precise map of where the primary evidence sits.** It is not archival research. No carton has been opened. No archival reference has been invented to conceal that.

Its largest single weakness: **the Moroccan-side documentary base is currently zero.** Every dossier here describes Moroccan actors substantially through European reporting about them — including **Ma al-'Aynayn**, who was a prolific author, and **Abd el-Krim**, whose memoirs exist. Correcting this is not an enhancement. It is the difference between a history of Morocco and a history of what Europeans wrote down about Morocco.

> **The question the workspace is built to answer, applied to itself:** *what do we actually know, and how do we know it?* On present evidence, most of what is confidently repeated about nineteenth- and twentieth-century Morocco is known because a French or Spanish official wrote it in a report intended to justify what he was doing.
